text:
Ohio University, Athens, Ohio. (Photo by Ben Wirtz Siegel, courtesy of Ohio University.)As America celebrates its 250th birthday, small towns like Athens, Ohio, are global leaders and ambassadors.
In the Appalachian foothills, Athens was named a top-10 college town in the nation and the best college town in the Midwest in recent rankings. Athens, home of Ohio University, thrives on the global stage.
America at 250
Students at Ohio University here run an advertising agency called NEXT. Siemens, the multinational tech conglomerate, used the NEXT student ad agency to create video content highlighting the company’s long connection to America for the sesquicentennial. 
Company reps traveled to Athens from Atlanta, working with students and Ohio University’s new 21-by-12 foot LED video wall on campus. 
This wall, a high-tech screen, was made by Nvidia, an American technology company specializing in microchips and GPUs (graphics processing units).
Nvidia, created in 1993, is America’s most valuable company.
Global footprint
At graduate commencement on May 1, Ohio University bestowed a master’s degree on a Fulbright Scholar from Vietnam. 
After graduation from the Ohio University School of Media Arts and Studies (MDIA), he returned to Vietnam to teach university students about emerging technologies in communication and run a start-up company he co-founded.
Meanwhile, Ohio University graduate Maxwell Burton (Class of 2025 Journalism/Strategic Communication) received a Fulbright grant to teach English and U.S. culture in Taiwan.
World Cup soccer
The connections between small towns and the World Cup are virtually limitless. 
Jon Greenberg, who graduated from Ohio University a quarter-century ago, is founding editor and columnist at The Athletic. He covered the World Cup from Hershey, Pennsylvania (population approximately 14,000), birthplace of Team USA star Christian Pulisic, “Captain America.”
Getty Images’ photographers assigned to cover the World Cup included Sarah Stier and Emilee Chinn:

 Stier graduated from Archbishop Alter High School in Kettering in 2014 and Ohio University in 2018
Chinn graduated from Zane Trace High School in Chillicothe in 2016 and Ohio University in 2020

Pulitzer Prize winner from Malaysia
Born in Malaysia in 1984, Marcus Yam ventured to Ohio University to sharpen his photography skills. He won the 2022 Pulitzer Prize for Breaking New Photography for coverage of the chaotic U.S. exit from Afghanistan.
After winning the Pulitzer, Yam recalled his boot-camp-like training in Athens and the nearby hamlet of Shade. As a student at the School of Visual Communication, he drove to the unincorporated community south of Athens to compile his photo essay.
“That experience in Shade set the foundation for my career,” Yam said. “I had a sense of being unleashed. It gave me the confidence to go anywhere.”
Conclusion
Yes, the world can be dangerous and, yes, we continue to face herculean challenges of climate change, conflict, and more. 
But as America turns 250, let us remember and celebrate small towns like Athens that launch leaders into the world and welcome scholars from around the world.
Ken Klein is an Ohio University alumnus who worked for The Associated Press, Gannett, congressional staff, and a national trade association. Now retired, he volunteers as a research assistant for Ohio University.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Why elections mean faster state budgets in Pennsylvania
description: The vast majority of state budgets have been late during the past two decades in Pennsylvania – but in non-election years, negotiations drag on three times as long, according to an analysis by the Capital-Star.  This year, for example, with an election coming up for half the state Senate, the entire state House and […]
text:
Most state budgets have been late during the past 20 years in Pennsylvania. But in non-election years, negotiations go three times longer. (Photo by John L. Micek/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
 
The vast majority of state budgets have been late during the past two decades in Pennsylvania – but in non-election years, negotiations drag on three times as long, according to an analysis by the Capital-Star. 
This year, for example, with an election coming up for half the state Senate, the entire state House and the governor’s office, lawmakers approved a budget within two weeks of the June 30 deadline. That’s a dramatic departure from much of the recent past, including negotiations that went 135 days last year when none of those seats were up aside from a couple special elections. 
Several factors play into the election-year budget effect known to careful observers and many people who work in Harrisburg. The Capital-Star talked to several of them. 
Here are the main takeaways:
 It wasn’t always like this

During non-election years, it’s taken lawmakers about three times as long to negotiate state budgets, according to an analysis of the past two decades.
Prior to that, late budgets were rare in the commonwealth. Republicans held a trifecta for most of the decade leading up to the election of Gov. Ed Rendell in 2003. Since then, it’s been divided for all but four years under former Republican Gov. Tom Corbett.
But lawmakers and analysts say disagreements between a divided government is just one factor. 
“Under (GOP Gov. Tom) Ridge, they would resolve the budget by May,” said Sen. Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia). 
In fact, three budgets under Ridge were resolved in May. Two came together in June – and one in April. 
State Sen. Anthony Williams speaks at a rally in opposition to a tax on skill games held by the Pennsylvania Tavern and Players Association June 24, 2026. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
Williams assumed office in 1998, during Ridge’s first term. He succeeded his father the late Hardy Williams – who’d been in the legislature since his election to the state House in 1971 and went through a few budget impasses during the divided governments of Democratic Govs. Bob Casey Sr. and Milton Shapp. 
Williams noted late budgets became more frequent and dramatic at the beginning of Rendell’s term and escalated during Gov. Tom Wolf’s administration, coinciding with accelerated political polarization. 
“When I first arrived, … it wasn’t parties, it was about the institution,” he said. “The structure hasn’t changed dramatically. So, what’s the hold up other than partisan politics? It’s about power and party, not about substance. No one wants to risk putting their brand in a negative light.” 
And that’s exacerbated while candidates are seeking re-election. They want to avoid extended budget negotiations and any votes and debates that could be spun as controversial and provide fodder for opponents, experts say.
Former Gov. Tom Wolf speaks at Pennsylvania State Association of Township Supervisors (PSATS) annual conference in Hershey, April 21, 2015. Pennsylvania’s budget was last on time more than a decade ago, during the first term of Gov. Tom Wolf – when the commonwealth also endured its longest impasse of 270 days, overlapping with Wolf’s proposal for the next fiscal year. (Emily Previti)
Where compromise once might’ve been seen as an accomplishment, there’s a fear or belief that it could amount to a betrayal among voters in today’s political landscape. 
“Elected officials and elected leaders, the things they prioritize are different,” said Berwood Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research at Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster. “And I think there are legitimate differences in [policies], spending priorities and the belief in the role of government, state government particularly. … But it comes back to polarization and priorities” – both between and within parties.
Another factor in Pennsylvania: a late budget used to mean a government shutdown. But a 2009 state Supreme Court decision removed that from the equation with its ruling that state workers must be paid regardless of whether a current budget is in place. 
“Before you had this big lever, you had this big cudgel. ‘If we don’t pass this budget, all the state workers won’t get paid.’ And that was a pretty big deal,” said Republican strategist Christopher Nicholas. “It was a big hit to the Harrisburg economy because so many state employees are based here.”
So big, Nicholas recalled, that local banks created loan programs specifically for state workers during those earlier impasses. 
“Once they changed the law, it was like, ‘Yeah, whatever. You guys fight it out. I’m still getting my paycheck every two weeks,’” he said.
 Voters care (kind of)

And now, more than 15 years later? 
Budget season still matters to people in the capital region, Nicholas said, but not so much beyond that – for the most part.
“There’s a whole set of people here – legislators, lobbyists, maybe some members of the press – that make their vacation schedules based around what they think the state budget’s gonna be,” he  said. “If you go 50 miles from here and talk to a regular person, June 30th is not some super big date on their calendar.”
Whether it’s a major issue or not, polls suggest most voters have an opinion about who’s to blame when state budgets run late.

F&M’s Center for Opinion Research has polled representative samples of Pennsylvania voters during multiple impasses. 
Yost shared six sets of responses from 2007 through 2016. 
In each case, respondents could choose whether the governor or legislature was more at fault – or they could say they weren’t sure. Every time, more than half picked the legislature, about one-third chose the governor and the remainder indicated they did not know. 
In 2023, the choices were the governor, House Democrats and Senate Republicans. Nearly a third blamed the Senate GOP most, 20 percent each pointed at the governor and House Dems – and 28 percent responded they did not know.
 “The bottom line about the polling data is that there’s enough blame to go around,” Yost said. “And that governors typically aren’t the ones that are perceived as being the major problem.”
Gov. Josh Shapiro hold a piglet at the Pennsylvania Farm Show on Jan. 8, 2025 (Capital-Star photo by Ian Karbal)
Despite that, Williams believes Shapiro’s presidential ambitions provide motivation for the GOP to ensure the budget is late – even if only by a hair.
 “Josh Shapiro is viewed as a viable presidential candidate,” Williams said. “So even if it’s a day, a week or two late, they can say it’s late two, three years in a row – whatever it is.”
 Budget impasses rarely yield big benefits

Asked to identify a significant change, people interviewed for this story breakthrough or compromise coming out of drawn out budget negotiations over the years. 
They overwhelmingly pointed to the commonwealth legalizing casino gaming in 2004 as the biggest example. 
State Sen. Nikil Saval (D, Philadelphia) cited one that came up during the  2025 impasse. He  opposed it, but nonetheless recognizes its significance. 
“I didn’t support this, but the Republicans – and, indeed, some Democrats supported it as well – had a major breakthrough when they were able to get Pennsylvania to withdraw from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative,” Saval said. “That was one of the things that unlocked the rest of the budget [in 2025]. You could argue that that was a breakthrough.” 
Pennsylvanians are more immediately familiar with the costs of a late budget, having witnessed them last year. 
If budget negotiations drag on long enough, counties and schools might need to borrow money, siphon savings or pause programs. Some nonprofits, community service providers and other contractors similarly cut staff, services or even fold completely.
In a survey of nearly 200 community service organizations, the majority reported running through their contingency funds during the 2025 impasse. Close to half cut staff, workers’ hours and/or client services. And more than one quarter were grappling with losing federal funding simultaneously.
These impacts, however, take months to materialize, Nicholas noted, versus the immediate and relatively geographically concentrated effect of a state government shutdown at risk years ago but no longer.
Other issues, meanwhile, languish while the budget takes up much of the bandwidth at the Capitol  – unless they’re tied into the horse-trading of budget talks.
That was avoided this year, with campaign commitments looming on lawmakers’ summer calendars. 
 Is election-year efficiency rooted in self-interest?

Expediency during election-year budgeting is an “unspoken understanding,” said Saval, who’s midway through his second term, of election years.  
“Outside the building, it gets voiced more clearly: controversial issues, subjects that are the subject of deeply partisan negotiations, major budgetary items – a lot of those things tend to be avoided,” he said. “Expectations tend to get lowered early on – maybe even as early as the (governor’s) budget address in February – in terms of what we expect to address in a given cycle. People tend to be risk-averse. There is a strong desire on the part of those who face competitive elections in the fall to go home and campaign.” 
State Sen. Nikil Saval speaks at a June 26 rally for transit funding outside of the Independence Hall subway stop in Philadelphia. (Photo by Daniel Perrin/Inside Climate News)
Aside from scheduling, campaigns might consider the potential for longer negotiations to provide fodder for opponents, Nicholas said. 
Truncated talks come with a cost, too. 
“It ends up leading to deferred action on a number of key issues that might otherwise be addressed or at least broached,” Saval said. 
Saval and Sen. Katie Muth of Montgomery County were the only Democrats who voted against the budget, citing many of the same reasons. 
The Capital-Star reached out to nearly a dozen Republicans who voted against it. Some didn’t respond; representatives for others indicated they were unavailable. 
At the moment, there’s an opportunity to raise revenue in ways that aren’t controversial with most voters – and yet it didn’t happen, Saval noted, pointing to “missed opportunities” with digital ad taxes and data center regulation. 
Similarly, lawmakers did not address skill games regulations, despite being under a court order to do so by Oct. 13 and the need for the billion-dollar tax revenue stream it would provide. Instead, they balanced the budget on paper by deferring Medicaid expenses.
A convenience store in Pottsville, Schuylkill County, advertises skill games on March 12, 2026, (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“The (Pennsylvania) Supreme Court decision would give them cover to do that, and they didn’t take it – which surprised me,” said Yost, referring to the lobbying pressure in opposition. 
Apart from this year’s budget gap, new revenue is needed to fill in the corporate net income taxes that the commonwealth’s been phasing out, Yost said, adding to the state’s structural deficit. 
Not to mention tightening financial margins stemming from persistently high inflation, cumulative borrowing costs at all levels of government and other pressures in communities across the commonwealth – which, as is often the case, fall on constituents.
“It kind of slides by,” Yost said, “and no one’s held responsible.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida’s GOP primary for governor: Undignified. Unedifying. Flat-out godawful.
description: I know y’all would probably rather not talk about the Republican candidates for governor of Florida. However, distasteful as it is, we must: The primary is Aug. 18. Now, this family-friendly publication frowns on scatological language, so let’s just call the campaign unseemly. Undignified. Unedifying. Flat-out godawful. Rep. Byron Donalds is the frontrunner[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds outside the Florida House of Representatives Chambers on Thursday, April 3, 2025. (Photo by Christine Sexton/Florida Phoenix)I know y’all would probably rather not talk about the Republican candidates for governor of Florida.
However, distasteful as it is, we must: The primary is Aug. 18.
Now, this family-friendly publication frowns on scatological language, so let’s just call the campaign unseemly.
Undignified. Unedifying. Flat-out godawful.
Rep. Byron Donalds is the frontrunner by a mile, maybe two miles, polling at least 40 points ahead of his nearest rival, who is either (depending on the poll) Lt. Gov. Jay Collins or James Fishback, who calls himself a “businessman.”
Lower down the food chain, you’ve got a former speaker of the Florida House, a retired firefighter, an Auntie Anne’s pretzel franchise operator, and a guy who used to be a computer repair shop owner with several arrests for domestic abuse and child neglect.
There are others, but you’ve never heard of them and you never will.
Donalds has received the endorsement of the White House’s current occupant, the electoral equivalent of Willy Wonka’s Golden Ticket.
The Trump stamp of approval counts for a lot.
Look what it did for the unrepentant adulterer Ken Paxton in Texas. He was impeached by his own party, yet he beat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn.
Some wild-eyed Democrats dare hope they might pull off a win this year: fresh-faced Presbyterian seminarian James Talarico is gaining in the polls.
But y’all: It’s Texas. A Dem hasn’t won there since the last Ice Age.
Here in Florida, the Dems are less embarrassing but also less likely to win anything, so we’ll talk about them another time.
For now, let’s concentrate on the GOP field.
Donalds has a built-in advantage, but also a few problems.
Spellcheck!
Remember the infamous Epstein “Birthday Book,” the one with the female torso and Donald Trump’s signature on her (ahem) pubic area?
Donalds leapt to Trump’s defense, assuring the world there was NO WAY that was Trump’s signature. He, Byron Donalds, had witnessed the man signing a gazillion things and that sig was just WRONG.
Except it wasn’t wrong.
Donalds would do better to just shut up about this can of worms.
He might also try hiring literate aides.
Pushing an education program he calls “Read to Succeed” on Instagram, he appeared before a sign reading “Achieveability.”
Spellcheck, congressman, Spellcheck!
One citizen wondered, “Is his staff just stupid, or do they hate him?”
Sad!
Then there are his policy positions, which are, shall we say, flexible.
An aerial view shows a data center situated near single-family homes in Stone Ridge, Va., last year. Local communities around the country are seeking more input on where and how data centers are built. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
He used to be all rah-rah about AI data centers, which his Big Uncool Friend Donald Trump calls “money machines.”
Thing is, Floridians don’t like data centers. According to a recent poll, 68% of us say “Hell, no!” to a data center anywhere near us.
Donalds finally noticed. He now expresses “concerns,” claiming he favors local governments’ ability to regulate these habitat-wrecking, water-greedy, grid-busting monsters, and has filed a bill in Congress to force them to get water and electricity from private sources, or manufacture power and water themselves.
(Not sure how people can manufacture water, but hey, Musk, Altman, et al. are supposed to be “geniuses,” so maybe they’ll figure it out).
It doesn’t matter, though. That bill will die on the vine.
Moreover, Donalds has received hundreds of thousands in campaign cash from tech moguls and data center builders.
Quiet part out loud 
Rival candidate James Fishback, who also says he has reservations about AI farms, pounced on Donalds like a squirrel on a doughnut, claiming Donalds wants to build data centers on “pristine land.”
Republican James Fishback announces he’s running for governor. (Photo courtesy of Fishback for Governor campaign)
Fishback’s barely polling in double figures; he needs more attention.
He’s getting it, too, largely by being, shall we say, racially insensitive?
He’s said Byron Donalds is a “slave,” and called him “Byrone.”
He suggested a black man be “lynched” for asking him uncomfortable questions about alleged sex with an underage girl.
That’s not all, y’all: He’s playing footsie with antisemites, too!
“AIPAC Shakur” is another one of his pet names for Donalds.
Fishback agrees with the unlovely and untalented white supremacist Nick Fuentes, who says, “Jews are running society. Women need to shut the [expletive] up. Blacks need to be imprisoned for the most part.”
We won’t go into too much detail about Fishback’s bizarre, somewhat troubling relationships with women (see underage above), but it’s worth noting that on May 23 he married one Valeria Quimby.
A mere couple of months ago, he presented a very different girlfriend to the public, one Francesca Raine, AKA “Crypto Barbie.”
Ms. Raine is unimpressed with how her former squeeze is handling all this, accusing him of ditching her for some “random girl after political pressure.”
Ah, young love.
A little more seriously, as of last week it was unclear whether Fishback would even be allowed to run in the August primary.
Seems in 2020, he lived and voted in Washington, D.C. Florida law says if you want to run for governor, you have to have been resident in the state for seven years.
Oops.
Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, jockeying with Fishback for second place, sued, pointing out Fishback was not, in fact, a Florida resident and should be booted off the ballot.
Lucky for him, a Leon County judge let him stay, suggesting because Fishback says he lives in Florida, he lives in Florida: “This Court will not be deciding the race between the Lieutenant Governor and Mr. Fishback. That will be in the very sound hands of the voters.”
Fishback crowed about his triumph over Collins’ and Donalds’ “lawfare” attack on him.
In response, Collins’ lawyer sniffed, “Who wants to vote for a candidate whose own sworn testimony is he committed mortgage fraud and doesn’t understand how the law works when it comes to election integrity and paying state income taxes?”
Where’s the DeSantis endorsement?
And what of Jay Collins himself? He’s still on the ballot and, given Donalds’ gaffe-prone campaign and Fishback’s ick-factor, you would think he’d be gaining more traction with Florida conservatives.
Florida Lt. Gov. and gubernatorial candidate Jay Collins at the Sunshine State Showdown in Davie on June 27, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)
Collins is a decorated ex-Green Beret, rabid abortion opponent, and author of a bill that would have banned Pride flags at government buildings but allowed the Confederate battle flag (the bill was later withdrawn).
Like Donalds, Collins is adamant about forcing data centers to behave themselves vis à vis water and energy, but says moratoriums are “not the American way” — never mind that more than 20 localities have imposed them.
Collins says he’s running on a “Stop the Bullsh!t” campaign. Need I point out that AI oligarchs are epically full of the, er, bovine waste product?
It doesn’t matter, of course: We can leave Collins and Fishback to snipe amongst themselves.
Both are going to lose big.
Bad bromance
A more interesting line of inquiry is what Gov. Ron DeSantis will decide about who should replace him.
He has yet to endorse anyone.
DeSantis used to like Donalds but then Donalds, knowing his home-state governor was about to enter the 2024 presidential race, endorsed Donald Trump instead.
When Donalds tried to contact DeSantis, the governor wouldn’t take his calls, instead trying to convince Trump he was “unfit” to be Florida’s next chief executive.
Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins and Gov. Ron DeSantis in Hillsborough County on Aug. 13, 2025. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix).

The bromance is over. DeSantis is now in full diss-mode, pointing out Donalds can’t claim significant accomplishments: “You’ve got a guy like Byron, he just hasn’t been a part of any of the victories that we’ve had here over the left over these last years. He’s just not been a part of it.”


It’s not that DeSantis has overtly favored anyone else: He’s snubbing his lieutenant governor (whom he chose) and pretending Fishback doesn’t exist.

Maybe he’s too busy plotting another presidential run; maybe he’s trying to figure out how to make a living once he’s kicked out of his government housing; maybe he’s freaked out at the thought he’ll soon have no power; maybe he’s struggling to decide which candidate he despises most.
He’s not exactly behaving like a good Republican soldier. As one Tallahassee political insider said, “Ron is leaving without a lot of friends.”
He could influence the race if he chooses, but perhaps the three most likely candidates in the primary might prefer he ignores them.
I’m confident Donalds, Collins, and Fishback can find a way to alienate a lot of Floridians without his help.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT insurers deny adequate coverage for chronic illness
description: An estimated 74,000 CTresidents take high-cost biologics like adalimumab, and many of these people are facing choosing between their medication, rent or groceries.
text:
My husband has Crohn’s disease, an inflammatory bowel disease characterized by debilitating and sometimes life-threatening inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. It requires medical intervention, often including major surgery and biweekly infusions at a hospital or clinic. 
At the time of my husband’s diagnosis, a ground-breaking drug called Humira (adalimumab) had hit the market. The invention of Humira was a game-changer for people with Crohn’s and other serious autoimmune disorders, due to its efficacy and ease of at-home administration.
The catch: Humira is one of the most expensive drugs in the world. Before insurance payments, it could cost up to $7,000 per month. From 2002 to 2022, it used over 100 patents to maintain the exclusive right of manufacture for 20 years. During this time, its robust assistance program meant most patients paid nothing for the medication.
After its patents were exhausted, a range of generics, or biosimilars, were launched. This sounds like good news, right? Nope. While the generics have a lower price tag, ranging from $1.500 to $3.500/month, the cost is obviously still unaffordable for most people. That’s where insurance comes in, right?
 Not so fast. With the generics came the loss of comprehensive assistance programs. Because the astronomical cost of adalimumab puts it in the “specialty drugs” category, most insurers will only cover it at 50-70% after the deductible is met. This means patients are stuck with a $500+ copay after the relatively poor assistance coverage is capped, until they meet their yearly out-of-pocket maximum. 
My husband and I are on Connecticare marketplace insurance, because we are both contractors. Even with the lowest tier of available insurance, we pay about $1,300/month in premiums. This is already unaffordable for many families, a systemic problem that I will not be addressing here. Our individual out-of-pocket max is $9,200, or a total of $18,400 for our two-person family. With the cost of my husband’s medication and our premiums, we may pay up to $25,000 in healthcare costs per year, assuming I have no serious medical needs that year.
Compare this to the median per capita income in Connecticut, which is about $56,000. Some of these people are covered by Husky, which carries an individual income cap of just over $10,000/year. This means that a person on marketplace Connecticare who makes the median per capita income in Hartford County could pay almost 45% of their income per year toward medical expenses!
 We are extremely lucky to be in a position where we can technically afford these healthcare costs. However, others are not so fortunate, and some have to stop taking life-saving immunosuppressants because they simply cannot afford it. This is a serious injustice. 
 In addition to the cost, every month, my husband and many like him must spend hours on the phone convincing Connecticare to even send him his adalimumab to begin with. Three months into the year, he was forcibly switched from Hartford Healthcare’s specialty pharmacy to CVS specialty pharmacy, taking away his insurance advocate. He has had to take it late four months in a row because of this morbid version of phone tag.  
 While the arrival of generic adalimumab has reduced costs for insurers, it has increased costs for most consumers. One person my husband spoke to on the phone said, “The insurance companies don’t know what to do!” I would argue that yes, they do know the morally correct thing to do – they just don’t care. Their bottom line matters more than the lives of their customers. 
My husband is not the only person running into these exorbitant costs. Extrapolating from national statistics, approximately 74,000 Connecticut residents take high-cost biologics like adalimumab, and many of these people are facing choosing between their medication and, say, rent or groceries.
 To be honest, I couldn’t care less about the profits of the insurance companies. The CEO of Molina Healthcare, the parent company of Connecticare, made over $18 million in 2025, not counting stock options, of course. This salary could pay for an entire year’s worth of adalimumab for a thousand people! The entire system is rigged to harm, not help. When healthcare services are rendered for profit, the only people who win are rich executives, while the rest – especially those with chronic illness – suffer. 
Our legislators at both the state and national levels should be prioritizing this issue, not just for people on expensive specialty medications, but for all. Health insurance premiums alone are out of reach for a large number of Connecticut residents. Obviously, the sustainable solution is universal healthcare, paid for by taxes on millionaires and billionaires. In the meantime (since we know that’s not going to happen in our lifetimes), our lawmakers must force insurers to cap the amount they can extort from their customers. 
These medications are not luxury goods. They are a necessity for life. Allowing insurers to profit off of human suffering is unacceptable, and we must pressure our representatives to act.
Kim Adamski lives in West Hartford.

title: Fires destroy hundreds of structures in Spokane
description: Wildfires swept into Spokane on Saturday, burning hundreds of buildings in and around Washington’s second-largest city. About 700 structures, including homes, had been destroyed, according to an update Sunday morning from the Washington State Emergency Operations Center. The report said that more than 65,000 people were under evacuation orders. Officials war[...]
text:
People watch Old Trails Fire from W. Northwest Blvd., Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, in Spokane, Wash. (Photo by Young Kwak/AP)Wildfires swept into Spokane on Saturday, burning hundreds of buildings in and around Washington’s second-largest city.
About 700 structures, including homes, had been destroyed, according to an update Sunday morning from the Washington State Emergency Operations Center. The report said that more than 65,000 people were under evacuation orders.
Officials warned of extremely dangerous fire weather heading into the weekend, with dry conditions around the state and winds between 20 and 50 mph forecast east of the Cascades. Gov. Bob Ferguson on Saturday morning declared a statewide wildfire emergency and imposed a statewide burn ban.
“There is not a fire department in the U.S. that can handle a wind-driven event this size,” Assistant Spokane Fire Chief Lance Dahl said during a press briefing Saturday.
“There’s not enough staffing; there’s not enough people,” he said. “And if you look across the western United States now and you look across Washington state itself and how many acres are burning right now. The state resources are spread very, very thin.”
The Spokane Area Fires were more than 5,000 acres as of Sunday morning, according to InciWeb. Three fires are part of the incident: Autumn Lane, Fairview and Old Trails. Old Trails is the largest of the three, burning more than 3,000 acres.
California Interagency Incident Management Team 7 took command of the fire on Sunday morning. “This is still an active firefight,” Tom Stokesberry, a public information officer for the team, said in an interview with local television station KREM 2.
Stokesberry said the fires were the No. 1 wildfire fighting priority in the country.
The state Department of Natural Resources is involved in the response, along with local and federal agencies.
Courtney James, a Department of Natural Resources spokesperson, said by phone Sunday morning that the agency had dispatched four crews of around 10 people, six fire engines, 12 bulldozers and four aircraft to the blazes.
Ferguson, a first-term Democrat, was heading to Spokane on Sunday. A spokesperson for his office said he would get a briefing with officials at the city operations center around noon.
Republican U.S. Rep. Michael Baumgartner, who represents eastern Washington, during a meeting with local officials on Saturday, pointed to the bipartisan push to secure federal aid after severe flooding in Washington in December and said he expected a similar effort for the fires.
On Sunday, in a social media post, the first-term congressman said he had briefed Homeland Secretary Markwayne Mullin on the fire situation and discussed potential federal support.
The Department of Natural Resources said Friday that roughly 425,000 acres had already burned in Washington this year. August is typically the state’s driest month, raising fire risks. 
Public Lands Commissioner Dave Upthegrove told the Standard on Friday that state resources were getting stretched. “This is an extraordinary fire season that’s creating unusual challenges,” he said.
State Rep. Jim Walsh, who chairs the Washington State Republican Party and represents a district in western Washington, lashed out on social media Saturday night, arguing Democratic leaders past and present are responsible for the conditions that fueled the blaze.
“This is what happens when the state mismanages public lands for two generations,” he wrote, suggesting that Democratic officials were overstating how much climate change was a factor in the fires. “They’re trying to shift blame from their own disastrous policies. Don’t let them.”
The blazes come as the state’s primary election approaches on Tuesday.
A spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office said as of Sunday morning they had received no reports of damaged ballot drop boxes and no interruptions to postal services.
“While voting may not be the first thing on people’s minds as they respond to these wildfires, I want to ensure everyone has the opportunity to vote if they’re able,” Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a statement.
Hobbs emphasized that voters can return their ballot to any county drop box or elections office and can print replacement ballots online at VoteWA.gov, or visit county elections offices or voting centers to request a replacement ballot.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: ‘I have no reason to quit’: South Dakota EMTs still lending a hand in their 80s
description: When he first earned his emergency medical technician certification almost three decades ago, Gerald Frame didn’t expect to still be a volunteer EMT at age 83. He’s also still running an auto mechanic shop. “Who knew?” he said. “That’s my life. My world is pretty small — it’s the ambulance and it’s the customers that […]
text:
Gerald Frame, 83, stands outside of his auto repair shop in Whitewood, South Dakota. He's owned the shop since 1980 and has volunteered on the town's ambulance crew since 1997. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)
https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/EMS-FEATURE-WEB.wav
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. For broadcasters: See below for downloadable version with host scripts.
When he first earned his emergency medical technician certification almost three decades ago, Gerald Frame didn’t expect to still be a volunteer EMT at age 83.
He’s also still running an auto mechanic shop.
“Who knew?” he said. “That’s my life. My world is pretty small — it’s the ambulance and it’s the customers that I do repairs for.”
South Dakota’s emergency medical services workforce is aging, according to data gathered by the state Department of Health. The average age of an EMS provider in the state is 51 years old. More than 30 providers are in their 70s, and two of the oldest are 83: Frame and Jim Wallace, who both volunteer in western South Dakota.
Frame volunteers in the small town of Whitewood, where his mechanic shop is located and where the ambulance service is affiliated with the one in Spearfish.
Frame’s journey in emergency medical services started in the 1990s when he heard about an EMT class in Whitewood.
“And I thought, ‘what the heck?’” he said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
More than a decade ago, Frame had a heart attack. It was the executive director of the Spearfish Ambulance Service, Brian Hambek, who recognized the symptoms.
“So, for this last 11 years or so, I’m paying it back,” Frame said. “I got some help when I needed it, I like to help people, so in a way, it’s kind of paying back for my heart, him catching my heart attack.”
Hambek is glad to have him.
“Gerald is 83, but he’s spry as a billy goat, and I love him to death,” Hambek said. “He’ll do anything for his community in Whitewood. He just will.”
These days, Frame mostly drives the ambulance, stocks it with supplies and does what he can to make patients feel safe and heard in an emergency, said Andy Binder, operations director for the Spearfish Ambulance Service.
“He’s found ways to continue doing what he can do,” Binder said. “Maybe he doesn’t get to go carry the patient out of the ditch, but that doesn’t mean that he can’t drive the truck perfectly safe. It doesn’t mean he can’t do a good assessment and do vitals.”
Frame has no plans to stop.
“I have no reason to quit,” he said. “If I can continue to do it, I’ll continue to do this.”
Staying involved as a trainer
An hour southeast of Spearfish, 83-year-old Jim Wallace teaches scuba diving classes at his shop in Rapid City. He also teaches EMT courses in Spearfish and volunteers for the Spearfish Ambulance Service when he can.
“I’m in it just to keep my certifications up and better my knowledge, because everything changes constantly,” Wallace said. “I’m constantly learning, and that’s what I love.”

Jim Wallace, 83, is pictured in his Rapid City dive shop. He’s volunteered with the Spearfish Ambulance Service for over a decade. (Photo by Meghan O’Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)

Wallace first earned an EMT certification in the 1970s as a member of the U.S. Coast Guard. He served as a volunteer EMT in Clark, near Watertown in northeast South Dakota, after he retired. He and his wife moved to Rapid City 12 years ago.
After taking a refresher course with Hambek, Wallace started volunteering with Spearfish while he and his wife worked on moving west. He’d travel across the state — nearly 350 miles — to Spearfish on a Monday and stay all week before returning home to Clark, with a few weeks off in between.
“That’s how much I like being a paramedic,” Wallace said. “I’ll keep on doing it until I’m pushing daisies up.”
While running a dive shop, Wallace sometimes struggles to find time for volunteering in the field. But he makes sure his presence is there in the classroom, teaching new EMTs and seasoned veterans.
“He does all of my EMT education through here. That’s a way of him being a paramedic,” Hambek said. “He can help out and help train new people in this profession.”
Navigating challenges in rural areas
Black Hills State University is in Spearfish, and some college students take Wallace’s classes, whether it’s because they’re merely interested in getting their certification or because they need it for ski patrol or Forest Service jobs in the Black Hills, Hambek said.
“They’ll stick around for two, three years, until they graduate college, and then they’re gone,” Hambek said. “But at least I have them for a couple years.”
The flight of younger residents from rural areas is part of the reason for South Dakota’s aging emergency medical services workforce. The remaining people in rural areas might not have enough time to commit to coursework.
Some services pay their staff, but for some people, the pay is not worth the demanding aspects of the job.

The Spearfish Ambulance responds to about 250 calls a month and supports nearby towns with smaller services. (Photo by Meghan O’Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)

If rural services don’t recruit more young providers, Hambek said, they’re at risk of closing their doors once providers retire or physically cannot provide care any longer. That means longer wait times for people to get help in an emergency situation.
“So it’s a never-ending circle downward, which is sad,” Hambek said.
Hambek’s Spearfish ambulance crew listens in to Whitewood’s radio, and sends backup if the crew needs it. The Spearfish service responds to calls in a 600-square-mile area, sometimes lending a hand to neighboring communities like St. Onge and Belle Fouche, along with Whitewood.
“If you’re a small town with only a handful of patients, you can’t pay a bunch of staff, but if you have enough calls that people can’t volunteer, then how do you cover that?” Binder said. “You end up with the guys that have been around forever, that stay around and keep going because they want to help their neighbors out.”
Paramedics usually leave that position after less than a decade, Hambek said, usually to move on to different healthcare professions.
Less than 25% of the state’s ambulance services rely solely on volunteers, according to the state Department of Health. Others pay for part-time help. In Whitewood, for example, part-time EMTs get paid about $20 per hour, just for the time that it takes to respond to a call. In Spearfish, where call volumes are much higher, EMTs get paid for the entire time they’re on call, at about $15 per hour.
Wages vary across the state, Hambek said, depending on call volumes and staffing levels.
To get the money for wages and salaries, services say they need higher reimbursement rates from insurance companies and Medicaid. In smaller communities, providers might only respond to about 100 calls a year — less than half of what Spearfish does in a month, Hambek said.
“That means there’s income coming into the service, that I can afford to pay people to do the job,” he said of the Spearfish service. “But these smaller communities, they just don’t have the resources, both manpower and financial. And they’re tied. They’re linked together.”
Lawmakers seeking solutions
An 11-member legislative task force is spending time this summer learning more about how to support and fund local emergency medical services.
At its first meeting in June, healthcare leaders in the state told lawmakers they’re looking at regionalization as a possible solution to the shrinking EMS workforce, creating “workforce pools” so EMS leaders can rely on other services from neighboring areas when needed.
Lawmakers look for ways to deliver on support for ‘essential’ ambulance service

Bridget Hathaway, of the Jones County Ambulance, compared the approach to travel nursing. It could help services like Jones County “who are on the smaller side and might just need somebody for a couple days once in a while,” like during the summertime, she said, when communities often have more outdoor activities and celebrations.
In smaller communities with older providers, state EMS Director Marty Link said, a solution might require “having the tough conversation to say, is it sustainable?”
“That might mean that ambulance service does dissolve,” Link said. “And that might mean they can still provide service to their community, but maybe more as a first response unit.”
That would involve coordination with bigger communities to step in if a patient needs transportation to a hospital.
Lawmakers on the task force have until November to provide proposals that could be introduced as bills in next year’s legislative session, which begins in January. The task force’s second meeting is scheduled for Aug. 24.

title: Why Vermonters won’t call Fish and Wildlife about bears
description:
The department and the public it serves don't always see wildlife the same way.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Why Vermonters won’t call Fish and Wildlife about bears.
text:
Dear Editor,
A recent article in VTDigger provided good information about human encounters with bears. Mostly, though, it focused on comments by staff at the Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department complaining that people do not call them when they encounter bears.
In the article, it seems no one understands why people do not call the department when a bear gets into their garbage. Ironically, a letter published in VTDigger in May has already explained why, with supporting data. Walter Medwid provided data from an America’s Wildlife Values study, supported by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and led by Colorado State University, that surveyed Vermonters, with a separate survey of Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department staff.
These surveys showed the department and many Vermonters appear to be on opposite sides of core values. They think the department supports special interests like hunters more than it supports ordinary Vermonters.
The department bemoans the fact that people do not call them whenever a bear takes a birdfeeder. They ask people to report complaints. But when people do, the department uses those complaints to say that there are growing problems with bears, which it then uses to loosen the rules for killing them.
Some neighbors say they have regular encounters with bears taking garbage or birdfeeders, and they do not see it as a problem. They are not going to report it to the Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department because they think the department is not on their side.

READ MORE

The article said that 99% of the time when someone calls the department, killing the bear is not the first response. Sure. But it is an option chosen far too quickly, meaning bears are suffering because of human behavior. That is why people don’t want to call the department to report what are effectively non-issues with bears.
The killing of bears for simply acting like bears when people do irresponsible things, like not securing food, houses, cars and garbage, shows why Vermonters are right not to trust the system.
Mike Fry
Montpelier, Vt.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore touts friendship with GOP governor as he takes over national association
description: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore officially took over as National Governors Association chair Saturday, assuming the prominent position just ahead of a high-stakes national election that could reset the balance of power in Washington and across the states.
text:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D), at podium, takes over the National Governors Association chairmanship from from Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt (R), right, on Aug. 1, 2026. Chairmanship of the bipartisan organization shifts between parties every year. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)OKLAHOMA CITY — Maryland Gov. Wes Moore officially took over as chair of the National Governors Association on Saturday, assuming the prominent position just ahead of a high-stakes national election that could reset the balance of power in Washington and across the states.
Oklahoma’s Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt handed the gavel to Moore, a Democrat, on Saturday, at the capital city’s National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum. Over the course of the organization’s summer meeting here, the pair repeatedly touted their close personal friendship as a model for more civil public discourse in these politically divisive times.
“His friendship means a lot to me,” Stitt said. “And it’s not just up here on stage.”
Moore, who donned cowboy boots for his trek to Oklahoma, shared similar sentiments.
“We have had some really amazing times, but also just some really complicated times over this past year,” he said. “And I am so thankful, Kevin, that you were the one that helped lead us through it.”
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) donned cowboy boots for the National Governors Association meeting in Oklahoma, where he assumed the chairmanship from Gov. Kevin Stitt (R). (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)
Earlier this year, Stitt clashed with President Donald Trump, who sought to uninvite Democratic governors, including Moore, from a traditionally bipartisan meeting at the White House. Stitt called off that event, saying the National Governors Association could not facilitate a partisan meeting. Stitt still attended the White House event, recast as unaffiliated with the governors’ group.
This week in Oklahoma City, governors of both parties emphasized that their states are not the hotbed of political partisanship that defines Washington, D.C. Moore and Stitt repeatedly called for a political environment with more dignity and less division.
Moore is widely speculated as a potential future presidential candidate. On Friday, Kristen Welker, host of NBC’s Meet the Press, asked him whether a Democrat could win the party’s nomination in 2028 by leaning into the dignity message.
“Yes,” Moore said. “Because I think the vast majority of people in this country, they do not define themselves as a Democrat or Republican first. The majority of people don’t live like that.”
On Saturday, Moore launched a new NGA initiative called Service United, a bipartisan push for governors to develop state-based service programs modeled after the Service Year Option that he has championed in Maryland.
“Service United is a bipartisan call to governors to create and expand paid service programs in their states,” Moore said in his speech kicking off his chairmanship. “These programs will put people to work meeting urgent needs where those needs are. They will help people to build skills. They will help people to earn credentials. They will connect people with employers, and they will bring together Americans who might not otherwise even know each other.”
NGA secured $10 million from the Andrew Carnegie Foundation and the Schultz Family Foundation, to make grants available to states to plan or launch service programs. Moore said states will be able to apply for up to $1.5 million from the fund to build or expand service programs.
“Over the next year, I am asking every governor in this country, Democrat and Republican, for three things,” he said. “First, identify one urgent need in your state that paid service can help to meet. Two, build a model to recruit and support the next generation into this work. And three, make sure that the service for that young person leads somewhere.”
In addition to installing Moore as its next chair, the NGA installed Indiana Gov. Mike Braun (R) as vice chair and chairman-elect. Moore becomes the seventh Maryland governor to lead the organization since its 1908 founding, the most recent being Gov. Larry Hogan (R) in 2019-2020. The association includes governors from all 50 states and five U.S. territories.

title: World War II soldier’s remains returned home to Bennington
description:
Army Pfc. Bernard Sweet was 21 when he died in 1942 in a notorious Japanese prisoner of war camp, and his remains were only positively identified through a DNA match last year.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  World War II soldier’s remains returned home to Bennington.
text:
The recently identified remains of World War II soldier Bernard Sweet returned home to Bennington on Thursday, Aug. 30. Photo by Danny Zaffarano/Bennington Banner

This story by Jim Therrien was first published in the Bennington Banner on July 31, 2026.
BENNINGTON — The long journey of Bennington native Bernard Sweet, who died in the Philippines during World War II, came full circle on Thursday evening when his remains were escorted back to his hometown.
Army Pfc. Sweet was 21 when he died in 1942 in a notorious Japanese prisoner of war camp, and his remains were only positively identified through a DNA match last year.
He will be laid to rest after a graveside memorial on Aug. 8 in Park Lawn Cemetery.
Casket escorted
After Sweet’s casket was flown into Bradley International Airport in Connecticut, arriving from Hawaii, a large procession and escort formed up — including police agencies from Vermont and other states, veterans motorcycle groups and others — and proceeded north to Brattleboro and then west on Route 9 into Bennington.
Participants said that all along the route, especially in Vermont, people turned out, many with flags, to salute Sweet as the long procession passed.
Sweet’s official military escort was Brig. Gen. Sarah K. Albrycht, a Bennington native and provost marshal general of the Army.
“It’s an incredible honor; it is a sacred duty,” Albrycht said. “When I heard that we were bringing home Pfc. Sweet to Bennington, I thought, if there is ever anything I can do as a general officer, this is something to use my good for, to ask if I could bring him home.”
The process “felt full circle,” she said. “Pfc. Sweet’s life has ended, but his story didn’t. It’s continuing to now, and that’s incredible.”
Another aspect for her family, Albrycht said, “is that my mother’s cousin, First Lieutenant John Lahey, also from Bennington, is also MIA from World War II. Just another connection to why it is so important that we honor this family, and I got to do this duty. It’s incredibly special.”
Albrycht said she was “born and raised here,” and her mother, Mary Dermody, still lives in Bennington.
Speaking after the procession arrived in Bennington, Albrycht said, “We drove Pfc. Sweet across Vermont for the last hour and a half or so. We saw people coming out and honoring him, waving their flags — from all walks of life, all different backgrounds; and I think that’s the second part of Pfc. Sweet’s story. You know he was a hero. You know he endured the Bataan Death March; he was a prisoner of war; but his story continues, because now he represents what we never forget, which is we don’t leave our soldiers behind, and we continue to try to bring them home to their families.”
She added, “That is what the military does for its families, but it is also what we do as Americans in honoring people for the sacrifices that they make.”
Norm LeBlanc, commander of VFW Post 1332 in Bennington, who rode with the post’s motorcycle group, said, “I cannot say enough about the Connecticut, Massachusetts and Vermont law enforcement agencies, down to the state police, the county sheriffs and the local departments. We were with an escort from the minute we brought Mr. Sweet off the plane till we got here. … The coordination was really beautiful. There had to be a hundred people behind the scenes that helped this.”
He added that the procession continually passed people who saluted Sweet along the route, beginning on Interstate 91, but especially when they reached Vermont.
“People in cars would go by and hold their hand over their heart; truckers would salute and pull over,” he said. “And as soon as we got to Brattleboro, I don’t think we went three miles without someone standing on the side of the road the whole way back.”
Members of the Bennington VFW and American Legion Post 13 Riders groups were among those participating.
The procession reached Bennington and Devlin Funeral Home shortly after 8 p.m.
‘Touched the heart’
State Rep. Mary Morrissey of Bennington, who rode during the procession in a car with family members, said, “The day truly just touched the heart.”
The family car was behind the hearse, Morrissey said, “and we would drive through towns and people would be standing on the side of the road, sometimes at their businesses or their homes, or sometimes they would just pull off on the road, holding flags. Children and families; it was just all walks of life of people who stopped to honor this person who had endured so much in his service to our country.”
Sweet’s niece, Shirley McLenithan of Bennington, “almost couldn’t believe it, the outpouring of support and love and admiration,” Morrissey said. “It was just so touching.”
At the funeral home, McLenithan said she was “just overwhelmed” by the response of people she saw and felt unable to speak further at that moment.
It was McLenithan who answered a telephone call in August 2025 that informed her there had been a DNA match from a family member that positively identified Bernard Sweet after more than eight decades.
He initially was buried by the Japanese in a grave with other prisoners in the POW camp in the Philippines. After the war ended in 1945, the remains of U.S. personnel were taken to Manila, where initial attempts were made to make identifications.
In Sweet’s case, that proved impossible, his family was informed in a letter from the Army in 1950. But investigations by the Defense Department continued, and in recent decades DNA matches became available and the process has seen continual advances.
Sweet was identified through the work of the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency, which has a large facility in Honolulu.
Welcomed in Bennington
In Bennington, Sweet’s casket was transported to Devlin Funeral Home, the procession passing dozens of citizens and police, fire and emergency services personnel and vehicles lined along North Street where the funeral home is located.
According to a notification of his death published in July 1943 in the Bennington Banner, Sweet, 21, the son of Carl and Hazel (Ford) Sweet, was the town’s first reported death during the Second World War.
The Bennington High School graduate was said to have enlisted in the Army Air Forces in 1939 and had been sent to the Philippines to receive training in aviation mechanics.
He was posthumously awarded a Silver Star for bravery in defending the American military air base during the initial Japanese attack in December 1941, when, despite great personal risk, he maintained communications with other U.S. bases.
Following the surrender of the Philippines to the Japanese military in 1942, an estimated 12,000 American and 66,000 Filipino prisoners were force-marched about 65 miles as they were being transferred to prison camps. Thousands died or were killed and it became known as the Bataan Death March.
Bernard Sweet survived the march but died of dysentery in October 1942 at the Cabanatuan prison camp.

title: Local property dispute lands tea farmer in hot water
description:
BARRE — On a cool, damp morning in Barre, Amber Collett Terway harvested her resin calendula flowers with nothing but a plastic bin and her bare hands.  The sticky yellow flowers, valued for their medicinal properties, were destined for one of Terway’s “Quiet Mind” tea blends sold through her small-batch tea company, Tilia Tea.  The […]

text:
Amber Collett Terway, the owner of Tilia Tea, harvests calendula at her microfarm in Barre on July 31, 2026. Photo by Erin Petenko/VTDigger
BARRE — On a cool, damp morning in Barre, Amber Collett Terway harvested her resin calendula flowers with nothing but a plastic bin and her bare hands. 
The sticky yellow flowers, valued for their medicinal properties, were destined for one of Terway’s “Quiet Mind” tea blends sold through her small-batch tea company, Tilia Tea. 
The land she grows the flowers on came to her through an unusual arrangement: The property owner, who happens to be a member of the Barre City Council, allowed Terway to use the land for free in order to clean up the weeds and beautify the space. 
But it’s another one of Terway’s tiny farms, located on a city property bought out after a 2011 flood, that has caused confusion and contention in Barre. Some neighbors of the property on Hilltop Avenue say they were not properly given a say in what happened with the space before Terway started planting. 
Other neighborhood residents have defended Terway’s use of the property, saying that it elevates a former patch of grass into a chance to support local ecology and local business owners. 
The dispute over one small tea plot may prove a preview of bigger questions facing Barre — and communities across Vermont — as they contend with a growing inventory of vacant land left behind by repeated flooding. Barre alone has approved more than 20 post-flood buyouts that leave city-owned lots empty indefinitely. As officials weigh how to handle these spaces, and the businesses and residents who want a say in their use, the fight over Terway’s microfarm offers an early test of how towns will balance economic opportunity, neighborhood input and a transparent process.
Barre Mayor Thom Lauzon said he was “surprised” that the 0.3-acre Hilltop Avenue lot had led to so much passion and drawn attendees to city council meetings. But he said the issue of how to use city properties left vacant due to post-flood buyouts is likely to come up again. 
“If you were interviewing me after the 2023 flood, and you said, ‘Well, you know, Thom, how about if you create space that people can use for a tea company?’ I would have looked at you and said, ‘Why in the world would I do that?’” Lauzon said. “There’s a lot of uses, and again, that’s why you need the process.”
Herbs, holistic health and a hobby that grew
Terway said she has a “natural connection to farming” from her upbringing in Iowa, where her grandparents owned a farm. But she arrived at Tilia Tea Company through a rather winding route. 
As a community organizer in Minneapolis, she began sharing herbs with her friends to help ease the stress of working in activism. That led her to earn a master’s degree in holistic health, followed by a master’s in environmental science, where she studied urban re-greening efforts in Baltimore. 
So when she moved to Vermont, she expanded her garden as a way to connect with her young daughter — and gave some of her crop to her neighbors, who told her to try turning it into a business. 
Soon, she outgrew the available space on her property. That’s when Amanda Gustin, a Barre city councilor, mentioned that she had an overgrown patch of land Terway was welcome to use — and a new business opportunity was born. 

Tilia Tea’s Hilltop Avenue microfarm and the adjoining property in Barre on July 31, 2026. Photo by Erin Petenko/VTDigger

Terway now farms on four different plots in Barre, including the Hilltop Avenue lot under contention. She said via email that the total amount of land, combined, was probably less than one acre. 
“There are large tea and herb farms in Vermont that have 13 acres of herbs out there, and are doing a lot of bulk sales. But tea also works really well in small plots,” she said. 
Along with herbal tea plants, she grows edible flowers, catnip and some plants meant to absorb rainwater, help pollinators or make the plot more attractive for neighbors. She said she’s committed to making these plots, which she calls “microfarms,” a part of the community. 
“One thing that I do at the end of every harvest season, when we put in a new microfarm, is I host a neighborhood tea party,” she said. “So then all the neighbors can come and actually have a cup of tea on the land, and the tea has been grown right there.” 
A tea tizzy 
Terway lives in the neighborhood around Hilltop Avenue and had been passing the vacant city lot on her daily runs. The property suffered from a landslide from flooding in 2011, forcing the city to condemn an existing house and leave the lot vacant. 
She decided to reach out to then-city manager Nick Storellicastro this winter to see if the city would allow her to use it. 
“This seemed like a wonderful idea to both beautify a neighborhood and help a woman-owned business in Barre thrive,” Storellicastro said in a June 16 city council meeting. 
Storellicastro ran the decision past Vermont Emergency Management and approved her use of the property. Crucially, Terway told city councilors at a meeting Tuesday, Storellicastro emailed his confirmation but never signed a land-use agreement — something she normally does with landowners who let her use their property. 
She said she made sure to keep the neighbors informed about what she was planning. But Merrill Creagh, who owns the home directly to the left of the property, said she wasn’t aware of what was happening until she saw plastic tarp laid out all over it. 
“One of the neighbors came to me and said, ‘What’s with the plastic?’ And I was like, ‘I don’t know,’” Creagh told city councillors in June. 
Terway later reached out with a letter explaining her intentions and a batch of tea left in each neighbor’s mailbox. But Creagh said she still feels frustrated by the perception that the property had been “underutilized.”

Tilia Tea products sit on the shelf of the Barre Social Club in Barre. Photo by Erin Petenko/VTDigger

“Dog walkers, we all talk and (go) there, and so we didn’t feel it was underutilized,” she said. “So it’s an interpretation where a business wants to come in and grow their product, compared to the people who live there, and their historical knowledge.”
Creagh also said the city had asked local residents what they wanted for the property after the buyout in 2014, and the general agreement was that it would stay as it was, a greenspace covered in turf grass. 
The debate has left the city in a strange position. At Tuesday’s city council meeting, councilors and Lauzon generally agreed that the process Terway used was not transparent or official enough. 
“Even Nicholas (Storellicastro) didn’t deny that, in retrospect, he wished that it had come to the council,” Lauzon said. 
Yet as several councilors pointed out, Terway followed the process as it had been laid out for her at the time. And she’s already committed money and effort into the lot. She planted a cover crop of oats, peas and clover in order to restore the pH levels and introduce nitrogen into the soil. 
“The toothpaste is already out of the tube,” councilor Sonya Spaulding said.
“Don’t just leave it an ugly dirt lot”
Barre City was one of the hardest-hit communities in the 2023 flooding, particularly in the North End and other residential areas. That has left Barre in a difficult position: It has approved more than 20 buyouts, meaning that those properties, by federal rule, must remain vacant “forever,” Lauzon said. 
“I’m not a big fan of the buyout program because I don’t like the word ‘forever,’” Lauzon said. 
In addition to the hit to its property taxes, Barre must now decide how to prioritize its tight budget to maintain these new city properties. While the top priority is creating floodwater storage, that doesn’t mean they can’t become greenspaces, Lauzon said. 
“What I’d like to see happen is obviously maximize the flood mitigation value of the property, and then secondly, don’t just leave it an ugly dirt lot,” Lauzon said. “If it happens to be in an area where there’s not a lot of recreational opportunities, I think it would be great if we could create a little playground there or a little park where people can gather and use that property.”
He’s also preparing for the possibility that other businesses might show interest in buyout spaces. On Tuesday, the city council approved the formation of a committee to create a process for private use of public areas.
Lauzon gave the example of a dog training business that might want to use city property to host obedience classes. It could be a great opportunity for the city to get free mowing and encourage new economic growth — but the dog trainer should have to answer questions from the neighbors about noise levels and controlling unruly dogs. 
“Now, maybe I buy into your opposition, and maybe I don’t. But you’re sure going to have the opportunity to voice it,” Lauzon said. 
Meanwhile, there’s been some benefits to the drama for Terway. It’s drawn new interest and new offers from local landowners. 
“Folks have been like, ‘Wow, this looks really terrible for you. I am so sorry that you are experiencing this. I don’t want you to feel discouraged. Can you come farm on my land?’” she said. 
Most of those invitations haven’t panned out since she has specific requirements for the type of land she can farm on. But she’s still bolstered by the neighborhood support and the interest in her product, which has been selling out on her website. 
“I am barely keeping up with demand at this point, which is also I think a really lovely problem to have,” she said.

name: VTDigger
title: A Vermont farmer has a growing voice in Trump’s ‘Make America Healthy Again’ campaign
description:
John Klar of Brookfield was appointed to a national EPA advisory panel even as he and other MAHA advocates see some federal changes they oppose.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A Vermont farmer has a growing voice in Trump’s ‘Make America Healthy Again’ campaign.
text:
John Klar, a Brookfield farmer and conservative voice in Vermont politics, has garnered a growing role in the Make America Healthy Again movement. Klar is pictured at his home in June 2020. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
John Klar has long had a prominent and at times provocative voice in conservative politics in Vermont. But since Robert F. Kennedy Jr. became the U.S. health and human services secretary, the Brookfield cattle and sheep farmer has been finding a new, seemingly larger platform — as a supporter of Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” campaign.
Klar said his MAHA activism, which recently helped him get a seat on a Trump administration national advisory panel, focuses on removing pesticides and other chemicals from the food system and curbing the influence of large agricultural companies. That’s one piece of MAHA’s wide-ranging platform, though the movement is most commonly associated with skepticism or criticism of vaccines, a stance Kennedy championed in his previous role leading the nonprofit Children’s Health Defense. 
While MAHA-aligned views have had an elevated status in President Trump’s second term, some of the administration’s actions have clashed with the movement’s goals for cleaner food. Klar and other MAHA advocates have found themselves at the center of that conflict while Kennedy’s influence over U.S. public health policy only grows.
In July, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced it was appointing Klar to a panel tasked with advising the agency on federal policy that impacts farmers, ranchers and rural communities. The panel reports to Lee Zeldin, Trump’s EPA administrator. Klar was among 21 new members appointed to the panel, who hail from around the country and all serve as volunteers.
More than 90 people applied for a seat, according to an EPA press release. Klar was chosen, an EPA spokesperson said in an email, not just because of his farming experience but also his leadership in the MAHA movement.
“As EPA advances common-sense environmental policies, John’s perspective will support the Agency’s efforts to protect national resources, strengthen our rural economies, and help advance the President’s Make American Healthy Again approach to agriculture,” wrote Vikram Lakshmanan, the agency spokesperson. 
Klar’s appointment to the Farm, Ranch, and Rural Communities Federal Advisory Committee won’t be the first time he has had a direct line to EPA leaders.
Last fall, he was part of a group of MAHA advocates who traveled to Washington, D.C., to share concerns about the risks of pesticides with some of the agency’s top chemical safety officers. The meeting came as Trump’s EPA has proposed rolling back updates made by the Biden administration to how the federal government evaluates the safety risks of certain chemicals.
Klar summarized the meeting in a post on his personal Substack account, which has more than 25,000 subscribers and where he frequently writes about MAHA causes.
Earlier this year, the Trump administration backed the global pesticide maker Bayer in a case in which the U.S. Supreme Court ultimately agreed to shield the German company from liability for failing to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate, the active ingredient in the popular weedkiller Roundup.
The administration’s decision to back Bayer came after Trump signed an executive order invoking the Defense Production Act to expand U.S. manufacturing of glyphosate, which is one of the most commonly used herbicides in the U.S. and a key tool in many farm operations.
Both moves have angered many MAHA-aligned advocates. Klar, too, takes issue with them, though he said in an interview that his recent appointment to the EPA panel shows that the administration is committed to hearing from small, organic farmers like himself just as much as it hands major agricultural companies what they want.
“Those are signals that somebody is listening,” he said, adding that he thinks the president is “not totally captured by industrial interests — or he wouldn’t even throw us that bone.”
For years after Klar ran for governor in 2020, challenging Republican Gov. Phil Scott from the right, he was a near-ubiquitous conservative political presence, appearing at town halls targeting “critical race theory” and penning commentaries on right-leaning news websites. He voiced opposition to the Roe v. Wade decision, the Black Lives Matter movement and transgender rights, in one writing comparing supporters of the latter to Nazis. 
Klar also ran for an Orange County state Senate seat in 2022. He used a spat with the local school district over some of those same issues as fodder for his race, which he lost to the Democratic incumbent, Mark MacDonald. 
Klar made the case in an interview that he’s found a new political home in the MAHA movement. He dislikes that the movement is so heavily associated with Trump, saying its membership includes a wide range of political beliefs. He describes himself first and foremost as a supporter of Kennedy, not the president, though he appreciates how the president has given Kennedy’s ideas power and legitimacy.
“I work with Democrats every day, or former Democrats, or current Democrats. Many of them are very strong on the left right now,” Klar said. “We laugh about it. We may not agree on immigration or Israel, but we completely agree on healthier food and soils.”
It’s difficult to say how many people are aligned with the MAHA movement in Vermont, though Klar said he sees the state as fertile ground to grow it because of its emphasis on local food and small farms. He pointed to the passage this year of a state law banning the herbicide paraquat — the first policy of its kind in the nation — as evidence of growing awareness of the movement’s messaging. 
Victoria Dubin Master, a chiropractor who lives in Chester, serves as an unofficial leader of MAHA supporters in the state. She said in an interview that there are hundreds of people on an email listserv she runs to share information about MAHA-aligned causes. The group has regular meetings, though attendance can vary widely, she said.
Master helped organize an event at the Statehouse earlier this year featuring Mary Holland, CEO of the vaccine-skeptical children’s health organization that Kennedy previously led.
Klar is a frequent contributor to an online newsletter called The MAHA Report, which has about 275,000 subscribers according to its homepage on Substack. The newsletter is tied to a national MAHA advocacy group and describes its content as covering “food safety, scientific research, pharma influence, environmental toxins, and the political movement transforming American health.”
The EPA press release announcing Klar’s and others’ appointments to the advisory panel also described Klar as part of an organization called “MAHA Farmers Hub.” 
Klar declined to discuss the Farmers Hub in detail, saying it was still in a nascent stage and might launch more fully after this fall’s midterm elections. He said it was focused on “regenerative agriculture.”
Nevertheless, the EPA spokesperson said the organization “represents a key opportunity to network with and connect local New England producers to higher-level policy, support national health, and uplift healthier regional agricultural practices.”. 
Klar was adamant that while the MAHA movement has a wide range of sometimes disparate views, his primary focus is on supporting clean food that is grown locally and organically. While national polling shows the movement’s nutrition goals have broad support, other aspects are far more polarizing, including distrust of vaccines and a broad skepticism of the scientific establishment on many medical issues.
Klar said in a 2020 gubernatorial campaign debate that he was not opposed to vaccinations but that he firmly opposed the government making them mandatory.
“It’s not all about vaccines,” he said of MAHA in a recent interview.
“People might still argue about vaccine safety or efficacy. There’s just not as much bickering going on about healthy food,” he added. “And anyway, it should be music to progressives’ ears that some conservatives want healthier food too, right?”
