title: First week of third gasline special session ends with no action by Dunleavy or Alaska Legislature
description: The Alaska Legislature ended the first week of its third special session on the proposed trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline with no action. The session is for lawmakers to consider a property tax break to incentivize the proposed trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline, but Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who called the session and set the agenda, has yet […]
text:
The Alaska House of Representatives is seen on Friday, July 31, 2026, during a technical sesison. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Legislature ended the first week of its third special session on the proposed trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline with no action.
The session is for lawmakers to consider a property tax break to incentivize the proposed trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline, but Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who called the session and set the agenda, has yet to propose legislation for lawmakers to work on. 
The state House failed to pass a compromise bill earlier this month, during the second special session of 2026, after Dunleavy threatened to veto it. 
The governor has said he is holding closed-door negotiations to try to draft an alternative, but his office has released no details about those discussions.
Two members of the House and one member of the Senate held perfunctory “technical sessions” on Friday. 
Article II, Section 10 of the state constitution requires regular meetings unless lawmakers approve a resolution allowing a different schedule.
The House has scheduled another technical session for Monday morning, and the Senate has scheduled one for Tuesday morning.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho National Guard members have been deployed in D.C. since February
description: Members of the Idaho National Guard have been deployed in Washington, D.C., since February. Idaho officials did not previously make a public announcement about the deployment.  After a D.C. resident filed a $3 million legal claim this week against the Idaho National Guard for an incident that occurred at her home in May, the Idaho […]
text:
Idaho National Guard members conduct patrol operations in support of the DC Safe and Beautiful mission in Washington, D.C., Feb. 27. (Screenshot from D.C. Air National Guard video by Tech. Sgt. Melissa Sterling)Members of the Idaho National Guard have been deployed in Washington, D.C., since February. Idaho officials did not previously make a public announcement about the deployment. 
After a D.C. resident filed a $3 million legal claim this week against the Idaho National Guard for an incident that occurred at her home in May, the Idaho Capital Sun asked about how long troops from Idaho had been in the nation’s capital. 
Woman files $3 million claim against Idaho National Guard for detaining her in D.C.

“The D.C. mission was not publicly announced at the time because multiple Idaho National Guard mobilizations were occurring simultaneously, including an overseas deployment in support of combat operations,” Idaho National Guard spokesman Lt. Col. Chris Borders said in an email. “Given the heightened operational activity, the Idaho National Guard, in coordination with state and federal leadership, determined that publicly announcing troop movements would have increased operational security and force protection risks.” 
Airmen from the 124th Fighter Wing of the Idaho Air National Guard were deployed in late March and early April in support of military action in Iran, Borders told the Sun in April. 
Governors from multiple states, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands have sent National Guard troops to D.C. as part of a Joint Task Force-DC Mission in response to President Donald Trump’s executive order titled Making the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful. 
As of July 29, there were 99 Idaho National Guard soldiers in D.C., according to the Joint Task Force-DC website. 
The Joint Task Force posted a video of Idaho National Guard members patrolling D.C. on Feb. 27. The D.C. National Guard posted another video featuring two Idaho National Guard members on March 20.
The D.C. deployment is paid for with federal funds from the National Guard Bureau, Borders said. The Sun did not receive a response from the National Guard’s Joint Task Force about the cost in time for this story.
Gov. Brad Little’s office said in an emailed statement that he was proud of the support to the D.C. mission. 
“Governor Little is proud of Idaho’s citizen-soldiers and the professionalism, dedication, and service they bring to every mission, including Operation Safe and Beautiful,” Little’s Communication Director Emily Callihan said in an email.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Little’s election challengers criticize National Guard deployment 

After news broke of the legal claim out of D.C., Little’s November general election challengers criticized the deployment.
Former Idaho Supreme Court Justice John Stegner is running for governor as an independent candidate. (Photo courtesy of John Stegner)
“Why are our soldiers being sent away from home to do the federal government’s police work?” Independent candidate and former state Supreme Court Justice John Stegner wrote on Facebook on Thursday. “Why are they being put in situations that lead to confrontations with decorated veterans? And why didn’t we know this was happening?”
“I believe government should operate in the open, not in the shadows,” he said. 
Democrat Terri Pickens on Friday called on Little to bring the Idaho National Guard members home.
Terri Pickens is running for governor in the 2026 Democratic Primary election. (Photo courtesy of Terri Pickens)
“They should be nowhere near President Trump’s dangerous and divisive domestic adventures ahead of mid-term elections,” Pickens said in an emailed statement. “We’ll let the courts decide the merits of the $3 million lawsuit filed by a DC woman who claims she was arrested in her home by Idaho Guardsmen. However, if our troops were never loaned out to President Trump to ‘police’ D.C., they’d never have been exposed to this kind of liability.”
She argued more members of the Guard should be deployed to help with ongoing wildfires. Little on July 29 declared a wildfire disaster emergency and deployed the Idaho National Guard to help fight the Big Grass Fire burning along the border of Oregon and Idaho, the Sun previously reported. 
Borders told the Sun at the time that he didn’t know the specific number of troops that will be deployed. 
“All requests for Idaho National Guard support are routed from the requesting agency through the Idaho Office of Emergency Management to the Idaho National Guard,” Borders said at the time. “Our support, depending on the specific request, could include ground suppression operations like hand crews, heavy equipment and operators, logistics, sustainment and communications capabilities as well as traffic and access control, and evacuation support.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah won’t face mandatory cuts in feds’ new Colorado River proposal, but Lower Basin states could
description: After Colorado River states failed to reach a deal for sharing a dwindling water supply, the federal government released a plan for the next 10 years.
text:
The Colorado River is pictured near Moab on Sunday, Feb. 18, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)After Utah and six other states along the Colorado River failed to reach a deal on how to share its dwindling water supply, the federal government on Friday released its own 10-year outline. 


Colorado River Collaborative
This article is published through the Colorado River Collaborative, a solutions journalism initiative supported by the Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air at Utah State University. See all of our stories about how Utahns are impacted by the Colorado River at greatsaltlakenews.org/coloradoriver


Under the proposal from the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, the Lower Basin states of Arizona, California and Nevada would share in cuts of up to 3 million acre-feet per year. The framework doesn’t mandate cuts for Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming. 
Instead, it identifies a conservation goal for the Upper Basin — 200,000 acre-feet per year — about as much as Utah’s Deer Creek and East Canyon reservoirs together can hold. The plan would also allow for smaller annual releases from Lake Powell of down to 5 million acre-feet, compared to the current 6 million acre-feet, with new operating guidelines every two years. 
Utah’s chief Colorado River negotiator, Gene Shawcroft, praised the proposal on Friday, telling reporters it recognizes the reality of the water available, not just the demand. But he emphasized it provides a broad framework, with the details to follow in coming days. 
“I would just simply say, this is a bridge, not a destination,” Shawcroft said in a virtual news conference. “It certainly could be a bridge over troubled waters, but perhaps a bridge over no waters. We just aren’t quite sure.”
He and Amy Haas, executive director of the Colorado River Authority of Utah, were still reading through the 2,600 pages contained in the bureau’s environmental impact statement released Friday.  
Haas said the state will know more about what it’s contending with when it gets a copy of a two-year operations plan for 2027 and 2028 in coming days, though the exact timeline wasn’t clear.
The Colorado River is pictured where if flows near Hite, just beyond the upper reaches of Lake Powell, on Friday, Sept. 19, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
The Colorado River provides water to 40 million people across the U.S. and Mexico, contributing 27% of Utah’s water supply. It’s shrinking because of drought, overuse and hotter temperatures linked to climate change.
This year’s record-high temperatures and lowest snowpack on record aren’t helping. Normally, Colorado River runoff is about 13 million acre-feet, Shawcroft said. Now it’s 3.5 million acre-feet. 
He told reporters: “We’re in a dire situation.” 
On Friday, Arizona’s Department of Water Resources called the proposal’s cuts for the Lower Basin “unacceptable,” saying such reductions would devastate Arizona’s water users and its economy.”
The agency described negotiations over many months as “an exercise in lowering expectations, particularly for a long-term, seven-state agreement on operating this vital river system.” 
The disagreement could find its way into a courtroom soon. Arizona and Utah have both taken steps this year to build up litigation funds. 
“For Utah, litigation is never our plan A,” Haas told reporters Friday. “Whether it’s a plan B, depending on the context of this document, that remains to be seen. But litigation is not going to get us anywhere on this river. It’s not going to get us more water.” 
At issue in the negotiations is who absorbs necessary cuts. Upper Basin states argue they use less water than Lower Basin states, don’t have huge reservoirs to store water in dry years, and lack legal authority to place significant restrictions on water users. 
Boats can be seen at anchor at the Wahweap Marina in Lake Powell near Page, Arizona on Sunday, Feb. 2, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
The proposal out Friday is adaptable and allows the states to keep negotiating, said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum.  
“This framework provides the flexibility to respond to changing hydrologic conditions while preserving the opportunity for the Basin States to continue working toward durable, consensus-based solutions,” Burgum said in a statement. 
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, in a joint statement with his counterparts in the other upstream states, said they’re encouraged that incoming operating guidelines “will better reflect existing water supply, which must underpin any practicable plan going forward.” 
They went on to say that both the upper and lower divisions of the basin “are feeling the pain of severe drought. This is a reality that all states, and the federal government, will need to address practically, which is why a seven-state agreement will provide the best outcome for all water users in the Colorado River Basin.”
Water use is outpacing the river’s flows, and that overconsumption adds up. The combined amount of water in Lake Powell and Lake Mead is at its lowest point since before Glen Canyon Dam began to fill up in 1963, the bureau said in its Friday news release. 
If water levels dip to critical lows, as forecasts suggest they could by late this year, the nation’s two largest reservoirs could fail to produce power. If their depths continue to slide, they’ll fail to send water downstream. 
Conservation and recreation groups have called for an end to the gridlock, saying it’s dragging on in the background while hotter and drier conditions are driving up wildfire risks, air quality concerns and restrictions on the water supply.

title: Nevada faces ‘unrealistic reductions’ in ‘fundamentally flawed’ Colorado River plan, officials say
description: The federal government has released its long-awaited 10-year plan to manage worsening water shortages along the Colorado River, including deep cuts to Nevada’s allocation of the drought-stricken river.  Following months of negotiations — and years of states failing to reach an agreement on their own — the Bureau of Reclamation on Friday published a final env[...]
text:
The Colorado River is pictured just beyond the upper reaches of Lake Powell. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The federal government has released its long-awaited 10-year plan to manage worsening water shortages along the Colorado River, including deep cuts to Nevada’s allocation of the drought-stricken river. 
Following months of negotiations — and years of states failing to reach an agreement on their own — the Bureau of Reclamation on Friday published a final environmental impact statement laying out their framework for how to manage the river’s largest reservoirs,  Lakes Mead and Powell, after current guidelines expire in October. 
The proposal does not outline specific operating plans, but does call for the development of river operating plans every two years through 2036, unless the basin states reach a consensus agreement. The first of those plans for 2027 and 2028 will likely be released in the coming days.
“This framework provides the flexibility to respond to changing hydrologic conditions while preserving the opportunity for the basin states to continue working toward durable, consensus-based solutions,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in a statement.
The guidelines published Friday spared Nevada, Arizona, and California from the most severe water cutbacks that had been proposed over the course of negotiations, but called for Lower Basin states to reduce their water use by 130,000 acre-feet over the next two years, about 20% of the Lower Basin’s annual water use of 6.5 million acre-feet.
Under the federal plan, Lower Basin states could also be required to cut their use by as much as 3 million acre-feet annually during especially dry years. 
Nevada would face the lowest mandatory reductions on an acre-feet basis under the Bureau of Reclamation’s preferred method of managing the dwindling Lake Powell and Lake Mead. Nevada also has the smallest allocation of Colorado River water among the three lower basin states.
Nevada’s maximum curtailment during dry years would be 210,000acre-feet annually under the guidelines. 
Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo said the federal plan “seeks to impose unrealistic reductions on Nevada and our water users,” and “could have devastating economic and environmental impacts on Nevada.”
The governor called for “shared sacrifice from all water users across the Colorado River Basin.”
Upper Basin states – Colorado, New Mexico, Wyoming and Utah – will not be subject to mandatory water cutbacks under the plan, however, the plan does outline a range of reservoir releases in the upper Colorado River to protect downstream reservoirs from reaching critically low levels.
The final environmental impact statement instead sets a target for voluntary water cuts in Upper Basin states of up to 200,000 acre-feet, about 5% of the Upper Basin’s annual water use of 3.8 million acre-feet.
John Entsminger, Southern Nevada Water Authority General Manager and Nevada’s lead negotiator on the Colorado River, echoed the governor, saying that “any plan built around significant reductions for only three of the seven basin states that share the river is fundamentally flawed by its nature.”
“While our community is prepared to manage through short-term reductions to protect the Colorado River system, as the basin’s smallest water user, Nevada cannot solve the river’s imbalance alone,” Entsminger said. “Long-term solutions must recognize that the Colorado River’s challenges are basin-wide and require basin-wide participation.”
Lombardo and Entsminger said they remained committed to finding a seven-state consensus agreement.
The Upper Colorado River Commission said they are waiting on final reports to “provide a more comprehensive assessment of the federal operating plan,” but plan to impose mandatory cuts to water users and advance conservation programs to boost water storage in Upper Basin reservoirs.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: After fed report, Alaska pilots grapple with unanswered questions in tragic Nome crash
description: The National Transportation Safety Board on Thursday released the final report for the February 6, 2025, accident involving Bering Air flight 445 that killed all 10 people on board. While the NTSB’s report identifies airspeed and load issues as the main causes of the crash, the Alaska aviation community is still reeling over how it […]
text:
Empennage, or the tail of the plane, during post-recovery examination in Nome. (NTSB photo)The National Transportation Safety Board on Thursday released the final report for the February 6, 2025, accident involving Bering Air flight 445 that killed all 10 people on board. 
While the NTSB’s report identifies airspeed and load issues as the main causes of the crash, the Alaska aviation community is still reeling over how it could have happened with such a well-trained pilot from a company with an excellent safety record.
The Board determined the crash was caused by the pilot’s inadequate airspeed management and operation above gross weight. It also faulted the company for allowing overweight operations and the Federal Aviation Administration for inadequate oversight.
The Board’s team was composed primarily of investigators from outside the Alaska region, which is not uncommon when an accident is considered significant. But their lack of familiarity with the state’s aviation industry was evident in interviews as they sought to understand daily operations in rural Alaska. They also did not know about Bering Air’s unique reputation as, statistically, one of the safest small commuters in state history. 
While Alaska has had a challenging flight safety record for decades, that was not the case with Bering Air  prior to this accident. That is what has made the crash of flight 445 so shocking to the aviation community here, and has led it to more nuanced scrutiny into the cause of this crash. 
Airspeed
That February afternoon, Flight 445 departed Unalakleet for Nome at 2:37 p.m. in a Cessna Caravan. Pilot Chad Antill was not an inexperienced pilot, but he wasn’t a seasoned veteran either. He began flying for Bering Air in 2022 and had about 2,500 total hours of flight time with 1,060 hours in the Caravan — flight hours are incredibly subjective as a measure of experience and dependent on a variety of factors including the type of flying, type of aircraft and location. At 3:05 p.m. Nome reported light snow, broken ceiling at 2,700 ft, overcast ceiling at 5,500 ft, and visibility of 10 miles. An icing forecast issued at 1 p.m. noted constant moderate icing between 2,000 and 8,000 feet in the region. Trucks were active on the runway and taxiways to keep surfaces clear for landing aircraft.
Flight 445 initially proceeded without incident and at 3:11 p.m. the pilot contacted Anchorage Center while descending from 7,725 feet for Nome. At 3:13 p.m., according to data obtained after the accident from the onboard Garmin 1000 flight system, the aircraft was flying at 163 knots and 6,575 feet. The Anchorage controller notified Antill that Nome Flight Service was reporting the available runway was closed for 10 to 15 minutes for snow removal and he might want to slow a bit to “not get there too early.”     

U.S. Coast Guard rescue swimmers from Coast Guard Air Station Kodiak inspect the wreckage of a crashed plane near Nome, Alaska, Feb. 7, 2025. (U.S. Coast Guard photo courtesy of Air Station Kodiak)
 

The aircraft’s speed then decreased to 152 knots; it was reduced even further to 111 knots two minutes later — below the required Caravan speed of 120 knots for known icing conditions. At 3:16 p.m., Anchorage cleared the flight to descend at pilot’s discretion and maintain 4,000 feet. Antill gave a “good readback” of the instructions to the controller. Then, in one minute, things get out of control. At 3:19 p.m., the air speed briefly climbed to 121 knots; the aircraft was entering a rapid descent — an extremely dangerous situation. The last data point from the Garmin 1000 was at 3:20 p.m. when it reported 200 feet and 52 knots. The wreckage was later found about 34 miles from Nome on the sea ice.
Weight
In its investigation, the NTSB used data from several sources, including the Garmin, to conclude that the flight was about 800 pounds overweight out of Unalakleet for standard operations and 1,000 pounds overweight for flight into known icing conditions. There are different weight standards for flight into known icing conditions. Based on the Garmin data, the agency also asserted that flights on five previous days, which involved pilots other than Antill, were also overweight. That information generated significant attention when released to the public earlier this year, effectively directing the conversation onto fuel weight. 
Weight can become a factor in conjunction with some other event or action. For example, if the aircraft is loaded improperly, as in the 2013 Soldotna accident, or if an aircraft suffers a mechanical failure, or encounters severe weather conditions. 
It’s tough for FAA inspectors to check the weight on flights — they would need reasonable cause to unload the plane. The air service bears the responsibility for every load as it is company employees who manage those loads. For the FAA, Garmin data is not easily available, and absent reasonable cause an inspector cannot demand a company unload and weigh everything onboard an aircraft. This would be particularly onerous in Alaska where combinations of passengers, freight and mail are common. How the FAA can accomplish load oversight, without being unduly invasive on daily operations, is a question the NTSB is not required to address but the FAA will likely puzzle over for some time. 
It is indisputable Antill was flying heavier than his flight manifests reflected on February 6. While the Garmin 1000 is not infallible, based on the fuel weight he ordered when he departed Nome that morning and standard fuel burn calculations for his flight from there to St. Michael’s and then on to Unalakleet and back to Nome, the aircraft was overweight.
However,it is the air speed in icing conditions that should command the most attention from the report. Understanding air speed, many Alaska pilots say, far more than weight, is how to prevent future accidents like flight 445.
 
Flying in icing conditions
The Caravan was equipped with an aircraft deicing system, the Tecalemit-Kilfrost-Sheepbridge Stokes, named for the three British companies that first invented the process in 1942. The system, which is used to prevent ice from adhering to, and consequently building up on, wing surfaces and the tail assembly, is not designed for prolonged flight in icing conditions. Instead, it is intended to protect the aircraft while the pilot exits them. According to the Cessna Caravan Aircraft Flight Manual, even with the TKS deicing system on, the minimum air speed when icing has been encountered is 120 knots. From 3:15 p.m. until the crash, flight 445 failed to maintain that air speed. 
In NTSB interviews with several Bering pilots, management and the company’s FAA-assigned Principal Operations Inspector, the question of minimum air speed in icing conditions came up repeatedly. In each instance, the response was that 120 knots was the minimum acceptable. Not only was 120 knots listed in the Caravan manual but also in Bering Air’s checklist, standard operating procedures and its cold weather training materials. As one pilot told investigators, “…120 is what is the minimum recommended by Cessna so obviously that’s the minimum that would be recommended by the company.” 
To try and understand why Antill remained in icing conditions even as the aircraft slowed down, the TKS deicing system was discussed frequently in interviews. The regularity of icing forecasts in large swaths of Alaska was also addressed, along with the need for pilot reports to confirm or refute forecast validity. As the company’s operations inspector explained to investigators in the report: “We have forecast weather issues. Big State. Broad Forecast. Lots of changing weather.”  
Absent a confirmation pilot report, pilots depart into forecasted but not yet confirmed icing conditions. The TKS deicing system was designed exactly for this sort of potential icing environment. But, according to Chris Magerkurth, a former engineering specialist with Cessna who had seventeen years with the company working on ice protection systems, pilot over-reliance on systems like TKS is a concern. “The systems are designed to provide brief encounters with icing, not to hold or fly around indefinitely in any icing conditions,” he explained to me. “A pilot has no idea what ice conditions they are in or how quickly those conditions can change. They need to ask for a higher or lower altitude and get out of it.”

It is possible that the prevalence of icing conditions in the Norton Sound area has led to a subtle perception of the TKS deicing system as more “anti-ice” than “escape from ice” among pilots there. Coupled with the fact that many Alaska companies fly single-pilot aircraft, over-reliance on equipment like TKS while in tough conditions might be happening. This is especially true among the current generation of pilots who learned to fly in cockpit environments that emphasize automation. If anything is to be taken from this accident, many pilot sources stress, Cessna’s mandate to escape icing as quickly as possible would be the primary message, regardless of the accessibility to TKS.
In its recommendations, the NTSB called for the FAA to develop certain “surveillance criteria” for small commuter or charter services, known as Part 135 companies, who experience what the Board describes as “rapid growth, increased complexity of operations, accidents and/or incidents,” etc. But as he discussed with investigators, Bering Air’s operations inspector was physically present in Nome one week of nearly every month and the company had not markedly altered its route structure in recent years, even after the bankruptcy of Ravn Air Group in 2020. 
Further, based on a review of the NTSB’s database, Bering has maintained for decades the safest record among any small commuter or charter service of similar size in the state. Prior to flight 445, Bering was involved in seventeen accidents in the previous thirty-five years with only two in the previous ten years. There were no fatalities and only one serious injury when a passenger intentionally walked into a spinning propeller. In comparison, the company with the worst record in the period, Hageland Aviation Services, had 43 accidents before it went out of business in 2020 as part of Ravn Air. There were 29 fatalities and seven serious injuries in those crashes, its last occurring three months before the company shutdown. As Bering’s operations inspector noted to investigators, the company did not exhibit “risk indicators.”  That is part of what made the crash of flight 445 so shocking. Simply put, Alaskans did not see this one coming. 

Unanswered questions
A well-trained pilot with a seemingly reasonable amount of experience and reputation, according to his co-workers, for conservative flying, departed Unalakleet overweight into forecasted moderate icing conditions. He flew directly across Norton Sound rather than choosing one of Bering’s approved shore routes. When asked to “slow down a bit” by Anchorage Center he did not respond that conditions made such a request unacceptable. When told minutes later to descend at his discretion he agreed rather than ask for an immediate altitude out of the ice. He never declared an emergency. There is no record of him contacting Nome Flight Service to ask the trucks to leave the runway so his landing would not be delayed, which is a common request in such situations in Alaska. Finally, for several minutes his air speed steadily decreased and he appears to have done little to stop it, or to alert anyone that he was in trouble.
For people familiar with the aviation industry in Alaska, this behavior is troubling and frustrating to contemplate. In its recommendations the NTSB said nothing about further training in icing conditions. It is unclear what more could have been done to stress the importance of 120 knots in the Cessna Caravan. 
Magerkurth was part of the group that certified various anti-ice and deicing equipment over the years, including on the Cessna Caravan, and his thinking is quite straightforward: “The minimum icing air speed as set by the manufacturer is based on the changes in aerodynamic characteristics of the airframe such as drag created by various ice shape configurations,” he explained. “The company tests worst case scenarios based on the continuous maximum and intermittent maximum icing envelopes developed in federal regulations. When it sets an air speed limit, it is the result of that research.”

“The limit,” he said, “cannot be ignored.”
Editor’s note: The author worked with the principal operations inspector, who is a source in this story, at Larry’s Flying Service in Fairbanks in the 1990s.

title: Rep. Josh Turek holds affordability roundtable, criticizes Hinson for finances
description: Democrat Josh Turek said Friday he understands Iowans’ struggles with high costs of living more personally than his opponent for the U.S. Senate seat in November, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson. Turek, a Paralympian and current state representative, held a roundtable discussion with political leaders, teachers and small business owners at Dough Co. in Ankeny to […]
text:
Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat in 2026, spoke with small business owners, teachers and others about affordability at a roundtable event held at Dough Co. in Ankeny July 31, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democrat Josh Turek said Friday he understands Iowans’ struggles with high costs of living more personally than his opponent for the U.S. Senate seat in November, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson.
Turek, a Paralympian and current state representative, held a roundtable discussion with political leaders, teachers and small business owners at Dough Co. in Ankeny to discuss affordability — an issue he said was a top priority for his campaign and for most Iowans.
As a person who grew up in a working-class family, Turek said he understands the struggles that many Iowa families are facing as costs for housing, healthcare, insurance and other services rise while wages stagnate. He said “it’s working-class families like mine and a lot of yours that are paying the price for Washington corruption.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He asaid Hinson was one of the politicians currently making life unaffordable for regular Iowans.
“Washington is broken because people like Ashley Hinson are using their position to enrich themselves and their donors, not to fight for Iowans,” Turek said. “Since she got to Washington, D.C., Ashley Hinson has become up to 10 times more wealthy. … She’s voted four times in favor of the tariffs that are absolutely decimating our rural communities and our farmers. Six times voted in favor of this war, and  to continue the war in Iran, which is leading to increased cost of gas, diesel, and fertilizer. The bottom line is, I know that costs are way too damn high, and as your next senator, I am absolutely committed, laser-focused on bringing costs down.”
The Council Bluffs Democrat’s platform includes policies like raising the minimum wage, implementing a federal ban on price gouging for food, and reversing cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), made through Republicans’ 2025 tax and spending law, which Hinson and other members of Iowa’s all-GOP federal delegation voted to support.
One of the participants at the roundtable, Nathan Sage, had campaigned to become the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate seat, before ending his campaign and endorsing Turek. Sage said Hinson and others in D.C. are out of touch with the Iowans they represent, pointing to Hinson’s support for laws like the “One Big, Beautiful Bill” Act as well as her decision not to oppose the Iran war, as actions she has taken in the U.S. House that have directly led to higher healthcare costs and gas costs for Iowans.
“You keep seeing our leaders tell us, ‘a little bit of pain, for a little bit of pleasure, basically,” Sage said. “Like, we just got to deal with it. Well, it’s easy to do when you’re seated in power. It’s easy to do when you’re looking down at people and you don’t have to be on the ground with them. … But for people who are just trying to figure out how they’re going to pay their rent, how they’re going to pay for food on the table, how they’re going to buy school supplies, or how they’re just going to be able to live their life, extremely, it’s a major slap in the face.”
Evan Davis, co-owner of Dough Co. Pizza, said businesses are also struggling under the recent impacts of tariffs and rising costs. In addition to facing higher costs to run a business, Davis said affordability struggles are also hurting businesses like his because there are fewer people who have the resources to eat out at restaurants.
Others at the table said these are not issues Hinson understands, pointing to a Daily Mail report that found she spends $50,000 on a luxury apartment in Washington, D.C., and reports that her wealth has increased during her time serving in Congress in part because her husband did not divest from stock in his former company.
State Rep. Jennifer Konfrst, the former House minority leader, said Hinson’s campaign ads were “offensive,” as she was falsely presenting herself as a working-class Iowan, and as a candidate who opposes members of Congress from stock trading while in office.
“The  affordability cosplay that Ashley Hinson is putting on in that commercial and others is offensive,” Konfrst said. “It is offensive, because — don’t pretend to get our lives. Don’t pretend to be coming back here and living this life when we know you aren’t.”
Hinson’s campaign did not reply Friday to a request for a response. But in previous discussions on affordability, Hinson has highlighted positive impacts of measures like cutting taxes on tips and overtime as part of the GOP 2025 tax and spending law, which she argued have lowered costs for Iowans. A spokesperson for her campaign has also said Hinson is “working across the aisle to lower costs by taking on Big Pharma and Big health insurance,” and to provide “millions in funding for healthcare access and cancer research.”
But Turek argued both his background and his policy positions show he will be a more effective voice for working class Iowans if elected in 2026.
“You couldn’t have more of a distinction: A multimillionaire that is just up there, looking out for herself, for billionaires, for large corporations, for donors and lobbyists,” Turek said. “I’m running for the people of Iowa because I felt the same struggle that they have felt, and they deserve somebody, to have somebody go up there to work in a bipartisan way to to solve people’s problems.”

name: WyoFile
title: Ann Simpson, beloved matriarch, senator’s wife and Wyoming arts champion, dies at age 94
authors: Angus M. Thuermer Jr., Maggie Mullen, and Rebecca Huntington
description:
A ‘Greybull gal at heart,’ Ann and her husband, former U.S. Sen. Alan Simpson, had a powerful influence on and love for Wyoming through seven decades of marriage. 
The post Ann Simpson, beloved matriarch, senator’s wife and Wyoming arts champion, dies at age 94 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Ann Simpson died peacefully at 3 a.m. Friday just a day after the full buck moon.
“She was awash in moonlight,” her daughter, Sue Simpson Gallagher, said. 
“She looked good and at peace,” her son, Bill, said. 
The mother of three and the steady half of one of the state’s most prominent political couples and tireless Wyoming boosters, Ann Simpson died Friday at the Cody Regional Health Spirit Hospice House. She was 94.
“She didn’t wish to have any additional extraordinary care,” Bill said. “She was willing to have God take his course, and that’s what [he] did.”
But the loss is tremendous. 
“For all of us, her children and those whose lives she impacted, we are all heartbroken,” Sue said. “But our hearts are full of gratitude for this life well lived, this beautiful human being who enhanced the world and will continue to do so through her legacy of family and friendship and love.”
Ann and Alan Simpson on the back porch of their Cody home in August 2023. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Ann Schroll was the biggest catch on campus at the University of Wyoming, Pete Simpson said, when his little brother, Al, told Pete he intended to marry Ann. 
“I felt that he had lucked out,” Pete Simpson said at Al’s memorial service in Cody last year. “And look here. Look at this family. Look at this result, this legacy. Yeah, he lucked out, certainly we all did.”
Pete’s was one of many tributes to Ann, who was credited with supporting and stabilizing her husband and for being an unerring matriarch. 
“He could not have done it without her. She was the glue,” Bill Simpson said. “They really were a team. They were Ann and Al, Al and Ann. It wasn’t just Al Simpson.”

Alan and Ann Simpson not long after they were married. (Box 10449, Folder 3, Alan K. Simpson Papers, American Heritage Center, University of Wyoming)

Alan Simpson, the towering second son of one of Wyoming’s most prominent political families, was known for his across-the-aisle work as a Republican U.S. senator, spunky humor and larger-than-life personality. He died March 14, 2025, at his home in Cody at age 93. 
“He loved her dearly,” Bill Simpson said. When Al died, it was apparent it wouldn’t be too long before Ann would follow him. “They really couldn’t live without one another.”
A “Greybull gal at heart,” Ann was born 30 minutes after her twin sister, Nan Fogel Thorne, her son, Colin Simpson said, “I think somewhat to the surprise of her parents.” 
Thorne died last year. Ann’s older brother, Rob Schroll, an engineer, died several years ago. Ann idolized Rob, Colin said, and despite losing their father to a brain tumor when she was a teen, “she loved her childhood.” 
“She had some significant adversity in her young life that made her pretty darn tough,” Colin said. “And she never felt sorry for herself, and rarely did she let you feel sorry for yourself, which was a great way to live.”
After her father’s passing, the family moved to Laramie, where Ann attended high school and the University of Wyoming. All three siblings attended the university, where Ann earned a degree in education in the early 1950s. She taught third grade for a year before she married and loved teaching and learning, something she shared with her children, Sue said. 
She also loved the University of Wyoming Art Museum and leaves behind the legacy of the Ann Simpson Artmobile, which she started, Colin said, “because there were so many, so many children around Wyoming who didn’t have access to art.”
“And that was really one of her loves,” Colin said.
Ann Simpson and the Cody Fire District honor guard outside the Christ Episcopal Church in Cody for the March 31, 2025 funeral of her late husband, Alan Simpson. (Dewey Vanderhoff)
Ann often joined her husband as he toured foreign countries, dined with heads of state and traveled Wyoming to hear from constituents. 
The couple also championed Wyoming. When the Simpsons returned to Cody after Al served three terms in the U.S. Senate, Al and Ann poured their energy into bolstering Wyoming with contributions to institutions such as the Buffalo Bill Center of the West and the University of Wyoming. 
“She was ready to join dad and her sister, Nan, and her mom and her brother Rob and all her wonderful other relatives and friends,” Colin said. 
“She was a deeply Christian woman who loved God and knew that there was a better life ahead,” Colin said. “And she was always realistic about death. So that made it easier on all of us to understand that that was the natural flow of life.”

title: Prosecutors drop vandalism charges for Reflecting Pool damage, blame ‘contractor error’
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro moved Friday to dismiss charges against a former Olympian canoeist alleged to have damaged part of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.Pirro had charged David Hearn, of Bethesda, Maryland, with destruction of property of more than $1,000 for allegedly vandalizing the newly refinished Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on June 19. President Donald Trump, who has overseen the multi-million-dollar renovation of the Reflecting Pool, blamed vandals for damage to it.But in a 20-page motion to dismiss filed by the U.S. attorney’s office, Pirro said her office wouldn’t have sought charges if the Interior Department, which manages the Lincoln Memorial, had initially shared more information about repair work on the Reflecting Pool.Instead, the department only recently disclosed findings that Pirro said “strongly suggest that a rushed and botched installation by (Atlantic Industrial Coatings), the primary contractor, led to the damage to the lining of the Reflecting Pool.” That information was not known by prosecutors or the grand jury that returned an indictment of Hearn, she said.Information withheldShe said it was not until her office “reached out to DOI dozens and dozens of times that DOI slowly started trickling information to USAO-DC. Had DOI been forthcoming with the information clearly in its possession, the government would not have sought a grand jury indictment.”Pirro related: “Specifically, the newly released documents reveal that work on installing the lining almost immediately fell behind, due to a combination of very rainy and windy weather, repeated failures of testing on the sealing of the expansion joints, and delays in obtaining sealing product at the worksite. The rush to complete the project led to hasty and botched work that was not remediated before the project was finished and the fencing removed.”Pirro said that “almost immediately after work was initially completed, peeling was observed along the pool perimeter.” A National Park Service engineer's June 11, 2026, email “stated that the cause of the damage was contractor error via ‘overspray’; that the peeled lining would not float; and that the peeling would ‘not impact the strength of the liner,’” she said.“Moreover, the July 20, 2026, inspection by contractors confirmed that overspray and delamination had occurred, again pointing to contractor error,” Pirro said. “Finally, a recent visual inspection showed damage throughout the Reflecting Pool, even in the middle of the pool, where a vandal would not likely attempt to peel the lining. Given all of this newly discovered information, it is difficult to attribute the widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool to vandalism, let alone to establish that fact beyond a reasonable doubt.”Apology owed?Hearn on July 9 pleaded not guilty during a brief court hearing and was released on his own recognizance. His lawyers, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Fund, Mary Dohrmann of the Washington Litigation Group and Steve Levin of Steptoe LLP, said in a statement on Friday night that the government owes Hearn an apology for pursuing the case. “The Trump administration's case against Davey Hearn should have never been brought,” they said. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong. The government’s approach was ready, fire, aim. The administration owes Mr. Hearn an apology.”Hearn’s lawyers earlier this week had asked the judge in the case to release more information from the grand jury. They wrote in a motion that “the Government’s sole grand-jury witness on damages testified that the property was already damaged before Mr. Hearn allegedly touched it; that the same repairs would have been required regardless of Mr. Hearn’s conduct; and that he could not quantify any loss attributable to that conduct.” In a June 21 statement on its website, Atlantic Industrial Coatings defended its work on the Reflecting Pool.“Atlantic Industrial Coatings in conjunction with the US Park Service has identified some areas in the Reflecting Pool that require repairs. These areas are a very small part of the massive 7 acre project, and do not indicate a failure of the liner,” it said.“These repairs can not be made until the pool is drained. As soon as its feasible for the Park, the pool will be drained and AIC will be back to make those needed repairs as part of the warranty.”The company did not immediately return a request for comment. The Department of Interior also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Supreme Court tosses state regulator’s approval of Line 5 tunnel project
description: The Michigan Public Service Commission must revisit its order approving the Enbridge Energy Line 5 tunnel project because it did not properly examine environmental harms that might arise from extending the pipeline’s lifespan, the Michigan Supreme Court ruled Friday. The controversial pipeline runs from Superior, Wisconsin to Sarnia, Ontario, with a 4.5-mile[...]
text:
Laina G. StebbinsThe Michigan Public Service Commission must revisit its order approving the Enbridge Energy Line 5 tunnel project because it did not properly examine environmental harms that might arise from extending the pipeline’s lifespan, the Michigan Supreme Court ruled Friday.
The controversial pipeline runs from Superior, Wisconsin to Sarnia, Ontario, with a 4.5-mile segment of dual pipelines running through the Straits of Mackinac, where Lake Michigan and Lake Huron meet.
The decision written by Justice Elizabeth Welch was nearly unanimous — Justice Brian Zahra, the lone Republican-nominated justice, issued a dissent. Welch was joined by Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh and Justices Richard Bernstein, Kyra Harris Bolden, Kimberly Thomas and Noah Hood, all nominated or appointed by the Democratic Party.
Welch ultimately determined that the commission needed to assess the potential environmental harms in a new review, and compare those impacts with presented alternatives.
Line 5 | National Wildlife Federation
“The PSC must consider the extent to which the replacement project may pollute, impair, or destroy public trust resources,” Welch wrote.
The commission in December 2023 approved the project’s permit application, determining that the tunnel project would be the best available solution to mitigate concerns of an oil spill from the 4.5 mile-segment of dual pipelines running through the Straits of Mackinac. 

The Bay Mills Indian Community, Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians, Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians, and Nottawaseppi Huron Band of the Potawatomi and several environmental advocacy groups challenged the decision. 

They argued the commission failed to consider several alternatives to the Line 5 tunnel project, and that the commission had improperly limited the scope of its review by blocking parties from submitting evidence on the scope of the project’s environmental impacts and detailing whether there is a public need for the petroleum products Line 5 transports.

A Court of Appeals panel upheld the permit. The lawsuit rose to the Michigan Supreme Court, where the justices heard oral arguments in March.
Welch wrote that the commission also inconsistently considered greenhouse emissions from the pipeline as a whole in its harms analysis, and declined to consider other environmental risks — like oil spills — using that same scope.
“The inconsistencies in the PSC’s comparisons did not allow for such a ‘reasoned choice,’” Welch wrote. “The PSC incorrectly compared the environmental effects of alternatives that would fully replace Line 5 with the effects of the Replacement Project alone.”
Bay Mills Indian Community President Whitney Gravelle at a press conference held following arguments before Michigan Supreme Court on the Michigan Public Service Commission’s decision to permit Enbridge’s Line 5 tunnel project. March 11, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
The commission erred by failing to determine whether the project would pollute, impair, or destroy public trust resources, as well, Welch said.
As for the Court of Appeals’ error, Welch said the panel relied on state agency decision making, more specifically the commission’s Michigan Environmental Protection Act determination. It should have looked at the case without any deference toward the commission’s determination.
Bay Mills Indian Community President Whitney Gravelle said the ruling was “a reminder that when people stand together with courage and conviction, change is possible.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“For years, Tribal Nations, communities, and thousands of people across the country have raised their voices to protect the Great Lakes,” Gravelle said in a statement. “This decision gives us another opportunity to honor our treaty rights, protect our waters, and consider the generations who will inherit this place.”
Gravelle said the Straits of Mackinac were not simply a route for an oil pipeline “to be abused. They are sacred waters, the heart of creation for Anishinaabe people, and a source of life for millions.”
“Some things are simply too sacred to be buried beneath a tunnel,” Gravelle added. “Our work continues, and we remain committed to protecting the Great Lakes for generations to come.”
Earthjustice and the Native American Rights Fund represented the various Tribes in challenging the permit.
“This ruling is an inspiring victory for Tribes, environmental advocates, and everyday people who’ve joined hands in the fight to stop the dangerous Line 5 tunnel project,” Earthjustice Senior Attorney Adam Ratchenski said in a statement. “The Court’s decision upholds the bedrock principles of Michigan environmental law. Enbridge’s application to build the tunnel now heads back to the Michigan Public Service Commission, where we will be prepared with robust arguments in defense of Tribal rights and the Great Lakes.”

title: Controller declares ‘Idaho Transparency Month’ with stakeholder discussions, government access tips
description: August is now Idaho Transparency Month, according to a Friday announcement from Idaho State Controller Brandon Woolf. The initiative will highlight Idaho’s commitment to open government, with a focus on connecting Idahoans with the transparency platforms Idaho operates, the announcement said. The Office of the State Controller plans to hold stakeholder discu[...]
text:
Gov. Brad Little, left, and State Controller Brandon Woolf announce the new Townhall Idaho public meeting website on March 22, 2022, at the Idaho State Capitol. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)August is now Idaho Transparency Month, according to a Friday announcement from Idaho State Controller Brandon Woolf. The initiative will highlight Idaho’s commitment to open government, with a focus on connecting Idahoans with the transparency platforms Idaho operates, the announcement said.
The Office of the State Controller plans to hold stakeholder discussions, and share “Did You Know” transparency tips throughout August. In an effort to connect with Idaho residents directly, the office will also conduct man-on-the-street outreach about government transparency. 
As state controller, Woolf oversees statewide accounting, payroll and financial reporting. The state controller serves as Idaho’s chief fiscal officer and is responsible for ensuring financial transparency in the state’s government.
Idaho’s transparency platforms, including Transparent Idaho and Townhall Idaho, offer online searchable databases of public spending, financial reports, local government information, and public meetings.
“At a time when trust in government is under increasing pressure, transparency has never been more important,” Woolf said. “When government information is easy to find, easy to understand, and available to everyone, citizens are better equipped to participate in their communities and hold government accountable.”
Idaho ranks 27th in state by state financial transparency, according to a 2026 report from Truth in Accounting. The performance marks a 23-place drop from its rank at fourth best in the nation last year.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska has awarded roughly half of $218M in funds allotted for first year of rural health program
description: LINCOLN  — Nebraska so far has awarded nearly $100 million of its $218.5 million first-year allotment from a federal grant program aimed at filling healthcare gaps in rural communities. Ashley Newmyer, director of public health for the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, said Friday that puts the state in “good spot” in its […]
text:
The Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services releases a "dashboard tool" and provides an update on its first year implementing the federal Rural Health Transformation Program.  (Stock photo by IronHeart/Getty Images)LINCOLN  — Nebraska so far has awarded nearly $100 million of its $218.5 million first-year allotment from a federal grant program aimed at filling healthcare gaps in rural communities.
Ashley Newmyer, director of public health for the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, said Friday that puts the state in “good spot” in its overall implementation of the Rural Health Transformation Program. 
“We’re showing excellent progress compared to other states,” Newmyer said. “I feel good about where we’re headed.” 
Previously — and since December when the feds announced how much each state would get for its first year of a five-year RHTP rollout — Nebraska had not provided a tally of grants awarded. 
Nebraska secured the eighth-highest funding amount among the 50 states in that initial allocation round by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. First year grants are to be awarded by Oct. 31, Newmyer said.
Omaha dental school gets $4.6M nibble of $50B federal rural health fund

Newmyer spoke to the Nebraska Examiner a day after the state on Thursday publicly released its “RHTP dashboard” tool aimed at providing Nebraskans with information on the program’s progress and where resources are going.
The dashboard reflected funding awarded through July 7, so already was outdated. In the few weeks since, Nebraska went from having granted about $41 million statewide to $97.7 million, according to DHHS. The dashboard is to be updated monthly.
The “community health worker infrastructure” is an example of an effort bolstered by the federal grant funding, said Sara Morgan, deputy director of health promotion and prevention. That can involve local health departments hiring trusted community members to conduct home visits to help chronically ill people, essentially educating and ensuring that they keep up with care needed to thrive. Such jobs are more entry level positions that call for on-the-job training but not clinical degrees. 
“A big part of rural health transformation is helping Nebraskans keep care local,” Newmyer said. “We want to make sure that people have ready access to the care they need and we recognize we do have some shortage areas across the state.” 
In all, $50 billion in the rural health program was authorized under the mega tax and spending cut package President Donald Trump signed into law last July. That total is to be distributed by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services ($10 billion annually through fiscal year 2030) among states to help offset harm to rural areas due to sweeping cuts to Medicaid, the state-federal public health insurance for people with low incomes.
Half of the program funding is to be allocated evenly across states. The other half is to be doled out based on several factors, including a state’s rural population and policy actions.
Nebraska DHHS materials call the RHTP a “once-in-a-generation opportunity to modernize rural health care and make it more sustainable.”
DHHS described the dashboard as a step toward more “transparency and responsible stewardship” in how the state invests in health. Results can be filtered by geographic location. 
A feature DHHS health data expert Felicia Quintana-Zinn describes as one of the “coolest” allows a user to zoom in on their address and see nearby healthcare services. It provides drive times, in increments of 30, 60 and 90 minutes, to access various healthcare resources such as a birthing hospital or dentist.
The drive time or travel function also shines light on underserved areas. 
As such information is updated, Quintana-Zinn said, the dashboard will help showcase “how access to healthcare is changing over time with the work we are doing under the RHTP.”

title: ‘Truly dangerous’: Dry, windy forecast east of WA’s Cascades sparks dire wildfire warning
description: High winds in central and eastern Washington on Saturday could worsen large fires already burning in the region.  The National Weather Service issued a “Particularly Dangerous Situation” warning for Aug. 1, forecasting dry, hot and windy conditions in the region. Gusts up to 50 mph are expected in some areas.  The warning is the first […]
text:
The Sinlahekin fire in Okanogan County has burned over 24,000 acres and prompted level 3 evacuations. (Photo courtesy of the Washington State Department of Natural Resources)High winds in central and eastern Washington on Saturday could worsen large fires already burning in the region. 
The National Weather Service issued a “Particularly Dangerous Situation” warning for Aug. 1, forecasting dry, hot and windy conditions in the region. Gusts up to 50 mph are expected in some areas. 
The warning is the first of its kind to be issued in the Pacific Northwest. It’s one step higher than a red flag and came as more than 200,000 acres burned across 10 major fires in the region.
“These warnings are only issued when conditions are truly dangerous,” said Mason Friedman, smoke and fire meteorologist at the Department of Natural Resources. 
Washington Public Lands Commissioner Dave Upthegrove is urging residents to follow evacuation notices and use caution to prevent more fires from sparking. 
Over 426,000 acres have already burned in Washington this season, marking the fifth largest total acreage burned in a year this century, according to the agency. 
“And we’re just in July,” said Upthegrove. “This is an extraordinary fire season that’s creating unusual challenges.”
The state’s largest fire, Kaiser Canyon, has burned around 130,000 acres near Nespelem in Okanogan County.
On Friday, Upthegrove said Gov. Bob Ferguson had approved his request to deploy between 100 and 110 National Guard members with specialized training from the Department of Natural Resources to assist with firefighting. The members will deploy this weekend to the Little Giant Fire, which is burning about 30 miles northwest of Leavenworth, he said.
Federal personnel from the U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management are also responding to the fires. 
Upthegrove also said he’d recently freed up more employees from the Department of Natural Resources to shift from their usual duties to wildfire response as needed.
As of Friday, 1,038 wildfires were burning across the state, with 717 east of the Cascades, according to an agency spokesperson. Most are small, but there are ten major fires with the potential to spread over the weekend.  
The Department of Natural Resources and the National Guard have a combined 35 helicopters to aid the response. 
Washington state has brought in firefighting crews from dozens of states, along with teams from New Zealand and Australia.
“We have deployed all of our resources,” Upthegrove said. “But we are stretched thin.”

title: Governor grants Mitchell $1 million for industrial park
description: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden issued $1 million Friday from an economic development fund under his control to support an industrial and business park in Mitchell. The money comes from the Future Fund, which is built up through fees submitted by employers when they pay taxes to support unemployment benefits.  The governor awards the dollars […]
text:
Gov. Larry Rhoen cuts a ribbon with other state and local officials during the Mitchell High Plains Processing facility's grand opening on Sept. 9, 2025. On Friday, Rhoden awarded $1 million from a state fund for a Mitchell industrial and business park. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden issued $1 million Friday from an economic development fund under his control to support an industrial and business park in Mitchell.
The money comes from the Future Fund, which is built up through fees submitted by employers when they pay taxes to support unemployment benefits. 
The governor awards the dollars at his discretion, although a state law that took effect July 1 places new restrictions on the fund, including a more detailed description of acceptable uses and a requirement that awards must be recommended by the Governor’s Office of Economic Development.
The grant for Mitchell comes atop a $1 million loan from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and $1 million in local funding.
Governor awards $500,000 to program converting paraprofessionals to teachers

The Mitchell Area Development Corporation will use the money to prepare just over 18 acres of land on the south side of Interstate 90 on the western edge of town, installing utilities and roads.
That infrastructure is meant as an incentive for businesses considering expanding or locating in Mitchell, according to Development Corporation Director Mike Lauritsen.
“Once you put in the water, sewer and streets, it obviously becomes more attractive for businesses,” Lauritsen said of the land, which the corporation purchased three years ago. “We want to make it shovel-ready.”
Lauritsen said his office signed a detailed agreement with the state on the expectations for the project, which includes a payback provision if the park isn’t filled within 10 years of the infrastructure’s completion. Between the loan, local investment and the new dollars from Rhoden, Lauritsen said, the project is fully funded.
In a press release on the Future Fund award, Rhoden said the money would help Mitchell “attract new businesses, create quality jobs, and support long-term economic growth.”
Rhoden has awarded Future Fund dollars to several projects in 2026, including putting money recently toward funding for a program that creates a pathway for teaching certifications for paraprofessionals in K-12 schools.
