name: Alaska Beacon
title: Ranked-choice voting? Hold on. Alaskans have another ballot measure to decide first.
description: On Aug. 18, Alaskans will be asked if they want to change the way the state’s elections operate, but not in the way that most voters are thinking. The sole ballot measure before voters in the primary election would reimpose limits on the amount of money that individuals and groups can donate to political candidates […]
text:
A sample ballot seen at the headquarters of the Alaska Division of Elections on Thursday, July 9, 2026, shows the language for the campaign finance ballot measure. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)On Aug. 18, Alaskans will be asked if they want to change the way the state’s elections operate, but not in the way that most voters are thinking.
The sole ballot measure before voters in the primary election would reimpose limits on the amount of money that individuals and groups can donate to political candidates in state elections.
A well-funded campaign to repeal the state’s system of open primaries and a ranked choice general election — known as Ballot Measure 2 — won’t be voted on until November.
The measure on the ballot in August would prohibit political donors from giving a candidate more than $2,000 per election. Groups would be allowed to give no more than $4,000 per candidate per election.
Both limits would be adjusted for inflation every 10 years, and they would only apply to state-level elections — for governor, state House and state Senate.     
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 

Federal elections, those for President, U.S. Senate and U.S. House, operate under different limits enshrined in federal law.
A low-budget group called Citizens Against Money in Politics gathered tens of thousands of signatures in 2024 to put the newly proposed state limits on the ballot. 
In the state’s official election pamphlet, the chairs of the group — former state attorney general Bruce Botelho; Rep. Calvin Schrage, I-Anchorage; dog musher David Monson — state their case, explaining that they view campaign donation limits as “guardrails” on democracy.
“​​Without these guardrails, wealthy individuals and special interests can have an oversized impact and shift a candidate’s focus away from the constituents they are supposed to serve,” they wrote.
Speaking in a public hearing on Monday, Schrage said, “When a single donor can spend hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars on a single candidate, it creates a dangerous environment. It not only grants undue influence to the ultra-wealthy, but it also exposes our elected officials to the risk and perception of quid pro quo corruption.”
In the pamphlet, three Republicans, all former legislators, argue against the initiative.
“Campaign contributions are a form of political speech. To limit someone’s ability to support a candidate is to limit their voice in the democratic process,” said former Rep. Ben Carpenter, R-Nikiski; former Sen. David Wilson, R-Wasilla; and former Rep. Liz Vazquez, R-Anchorage.
In addition, imposing limits on outside donations gives an advantage to candidates who are wealthy enough to pay for their own campaigns, they said.
In Monday’s hearing, another Republican, Amy Demboski, spoke in support of their position.
“Reintroducing new caps creates a pay-to-play barrier where only those who already possess significant name recognition can thrive, effectively silencing the grassroots support necessary for insurgent or unconventional candidates,” she said.
The U.S. Supreme Court has previously ruled that it is unconstitutional to limit the amount of money that a candidate may spend on their own campaign. 
Ballot Measure 1 also does not limit the amount of money that a third-party group can independently spend to support or oppose a candidate. The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2010 decision, known as Citizens United, allows unlimited amounts of spending by groups that don’t coordinate directly with candidates.
Also this year, the Supreme Court ruled that political parties may spend unlimited amounts of money in coordination with federal candidates. That decision may affect state races in the future.
Ballot Measure 1 is the consequence of a lengthy and successful legal challenge by a group of Republicans inside and outside the state.
Until 2021, Alaska had some of America’s lowest limits on financial donations to candidates — $500 per candidate, per year. Those were installed by a 2006 ballot measure that passed with the support of 73% of participating voters. 
But a group of Republicans challenged the legality of those limits in 2015, arguing that they unduly restricted free speech. The case was appealed and remanded multiple times before a three-judge panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals struck down the limits in July 2021.
Gov. Mike Dunleavy declined to appeal the issue further, and the limits were removed ahead of Dunleavy’s successful re-election campaign the following year.
In 2022 and 2024, state lawmakers attempted but failed to pass a bill reimposing limits. Legislators this year passed a bill identical to Ballot Measure 1, but Gov. Mike Dunleavy vetoed that bill.
In his veto statement, the governor said the new limits “would radically tilt in the favor of the wealthy when it comes to elected office.”
The lack of limits has had its biggest effect on Alaska’s races for governor. In 2022, all three leading candidates — Dunleavy, independent Bill Walker and Democratic candidate Les Gara — recorded large contributions from individual donors. 
In this year’s race, the two leading Democratic candidates — Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich — have received large donations from out-of-state contributors. Both Democrats say they support passage of Ballot Measure 1. 
Most of the other 15 candidates in the governor race, including most of the Republicans, have taken similarly large donations, but not to the extent that the leading Democrats have.
The Republican candidate who has raised the most money, podiatrist Matt Heilala, has spent more than $1.25 million on his own campaign. Click Bishop, a Republican who has raised a middling amount of money, is also being boosted by a large union-funded third-party group. Those latter types of spending would not be affected by Ballot Measure 1.

title: Where Faith Meets Professional Care: Renewed Life Christian Counseling Center Brings Hope to Delaware Families
description: An integrated approach has made Renewed Life Christian Counseling Center a trusted resource not only for individuals and families, but also for churches throughout the region By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE When life feels overwhelming, finding the right counselor can be one of the most important decisions a person ever makes. text:
Photo Courtesy of Renewed Life Christian Counseling Center
 
An integrated approach has made Renewed Life Christian Counseling Center a trusted resource not only for individuals and families, but also for churches throughout the region
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
When life feels overwhelming, finding the right counselor can be one of the most important decisions a person ever makes. For nearly two decades, Renewed Life Christian Counseling Center has been helping individuals, couples and families throughout Delaware and nearby Maryland discover healing by combining professional mental health care with the timeless truths of Scripture.
Founded by licensed clinical social worker and ordained pastor Grant Hasty, the nonprofit counseling center was created to fill what he saw as an important need in the community.
After spending 18 years in pastoral ministry, Hasty recognized that many people were wrestling with challenges that required more than traditional pastoral counseling alone. While churches offered compassion and spiritual guidance, many pastors simply did not have the specialized clinical training or time to address complex mental health concerns. On the other hand, many professional counseling practices did not fully integrate a person’s Christian faith into the therapeutic process.
That realization inspired him to build something different.
“My goal was to have counselors who would come alongside people right where they are and help them in their time of need with the compassion of Christ,” Hasty said.
Today, that vision continues through Renewed Life Christian Counseling Center, which serves clients from four convenient Delaware locations while remaining committed to its mission of providing clinically sound, Biblically grounded counseling.
Hasty’s background uniquely prepared him for that role. In addition to earning a Master of Divinity degree and becoming an ordained pastor, he also completed a Master of Social Work degree specializing in mental health and chemical dependency. He is a Licensed Clinical Social Worker and, before opening the counseling center, served in four churches ranging in size from 300 members to more than 5,000.
His years in ministry gave him a front-row seat to the emotional struggles many people silently carry.
“We wanted to create a counseling center that has a passion for God, a passion for teens and their families, and a passion for healthy marriages,” Hasty said. “We also wanted to impact the local church by providing counseling that many pastors simply do not have the time or specialized training to address.”
That commitment has become increasingly important.
According to Hasty, the center continues to see growing numbers of clients seeking help for depression, anxiety, ADHD and addictions, including gambling and pornography. Counselors also work with people facing grief, marital struggles, divorce, workplace stress, unemployment, parenting challenges and school-related issues.
The uncertainty of recent years, combined with economic pressures and the everyday demands of modern life, has prompted many individuals and families to seek professional counseling for the first time.
One of the qualities that sets Renewed Life Christian Counseling Center apart is its whole-person approach to care.
Rather than focusing only on symptoms, counselors seek to understand the emotional, physical, intellectual, social and spiritual aspects of each person’s life. Therapy is designed to help clients develop healthier coping skills, strengthen relationships, gain new perspectives and deepen their relationship with God as they pursue emotional wellness.
Hasty is joined by a team of experienced counselors who share that philosophy. Along with Hasty, the counseling staff includes Ruth Burton, LCSW; Heather Baker, LPCMH, NCC; and Allen R. Harris, NCC, LPCMH, LCDP. Together, they offer professional counseling tailored to each individual’s unique circumstances and goals.
The center also works to clarify common misconceptions about Christian counseling.
Christian counseling is not judgmental, Hasty explained. Instead, it reflects God’s grace and compassion while helping clients navigate life’s challenges. It also differs from traditional pastoral counseling because licensed counselors utilize proven clinical techniques and evidence-based therapeutic approaches alongside Biblical principles.
Likewise, Christian counseling does not ask clients to set aside their faith in pursuit of emotional healing. Rather, it recognizes that professional mental health care and spiritual growth can work together to restore healthy relationships with God, self and others.
That integrated approach has made Renewed Life Christian Counseling Center a trusted resource not only for individuals and families, but also for churches throughout the region seeking reliable counseling referrals for members facing difficult circumstances.
To better serve the community, the center offers counseling services at four Delaware locations:

Reach Church, 2880 Summit Bridge Road in Bear
Brandywine Valley Church, 7 Mount Lebanon Road in Wilmington
Townsend Church, 4519 Dupont Parkway in Townsend
Still Water Farm Wellness Center, 286 Saw Mill Road in Townsend

By offering multiple locations, the center makes professional Christian counseling more accessible to residents across northern and central Delaware.
For Hasty, however, the mission has remained unchanged since the day the nonprofit first opened its doors.
His goal is to help people find hope in difficult seasons, experience genuine healing and discover the abundant life God desires for them. Those seeking more information or wishing to schedule an appointment can visit www.rlccc.org or call 302-464-0515.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Commercial speech lawsuit to proceed against major Kansas pet food company
description: TOPEKA — A federal appellate court revived a portion of a lawsuit that accuses Hill’s Pet Nutrition in Topeka of engaging in false advertising and orchestrating a misinformation campaign about an unsubstantiated animal health risk of pet food manufactured by rivals. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit, which includes Kansas, disagreed with […]
text:
The U.S. District Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit reverses, in part, dismissal of a class-action lawsuit against Hill's Pet Nutrition of Topeka that alleges the company undermined rivals with allegedly false information about the danger of certain dog food. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A federal appellate court revived a portion of a lawsuit that accuses Hill’s Pet Nutrition in Topeka of engaging in false advertising and orchestrating a misinformation campaign about an unsubstantiated animal health risk of pet food manufactured by rivals.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit, which includes Kansas, disagreed with a lower district court’s decision to dismiss the case against Hill’s filed in 2024 by KetoNatural Pet Foods. A portion of the claims made by KetoNatural were allowed to continue as part of a $2.6 billion class-action lawsuit.
Hill’s is a major manufacturer of dog food containing grain as a key ingredient, but the company’s market share softened from 2014 to 2017 with the rise of grain-free competitors, including KetoNatural. In response, KetoNatural asserts, Hill’s worked with Hill’s partner veterinarians and nonprofits to elevate an unproven theory that grain-free formulations of dog food increased pets’ risk for heart disease.
Hill’s strategy, the lawsuit claims, included use of marketing and promotional materials, including a website, to spread statements that plaintiffs contend violated federal law. In addition, the lawsuit accused Hill’s of manipulating the U.S. Food and Drug Administration into opening an inquiry into potential risks of feeding grain-free food to canines.
The controversy alarmed consumers and helped Hill’s regain market share from 2018 to 2022 while KetoNatural says its sales suffered despite the FDA’s decision data didn’t establish a link between pet food products and instances of dilated cardiomyopathy.
The lower district court rejected KetoNatural’s claim in the lawsuit that Hill’s should be held accountable for false advertising and be liable for false statements of alleged co-conspirators. The district court concluded the challenged statements weren’t literally false and shouldn’t be considered commercial speech under federal statute.
In a decision in mid-July, the Court of Appeals disagreed with the lower court by finding KetoNatural plausibly alleged certain information on Hill’s website and in Hill’s veterinary education materials amounted to commercial speech and could be false. The appellate court agreed with the district court’s dismissal of the plaintiff’s allegations relative to veterinarians and nonprofits associated with Hill’s, because those statements shouldn’t be viewed as commercial speech.
“KetoNatural has plausibly alleged that some statements and links on Hill’s’ webpages are commercial speech,” Court of Appeals Chief Judge Timothy Tymkovich said in the opinion written on behalf of a three-judge panel. “KetoNatural has also plausibly alleged that these statements are literally false.”
The Court of Appeals also remanded to the district court a civil conspiracy claim brought by the plaintiffs. This piece of the lawsuit is connected to allegations Hill’s worked with a network of veterinary researchers funded by Hill’s to gain traction for the grain-free diet scare.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: State of the race for U.S. Senate
description: Everyday voters are just starting to tune into the contest to replace U.S. Sen. Tina Smith. On the Democratic column of the primary ballot are U.S. Rep. Angie Craig and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who earned the DFL endorsement in May.  On the Republican column of the primary ballot are Michelle Tafoya, Royce White, and […]
text:
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (left) and U.S. Rep. Angie Craig (right). (Photos by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Everyday voters are just starting to tune into the contest to replace U.S. Sen. Tina Smith. On the Democratic column of the primary ballot are U.S. Rep. Angie Craig and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who earned the DFL endorsement in May. 
On the Republican column of the primary ballot are Michelle Tafoya, Royce White, and Adam Schwarze, who earned the GOP endorsement.
Minnesota last elected a GOP senator in 2002, when progressive U.S. Sen. Paul Wellstone was tragically killed in a plane crash and replaced on the general election ballot by the party with former Vice President Walter Mondale. Republican Norm Coleman won by 2.2 points.
The most recent 2026 polling — conducted for a consortium of news organizations by Mason-Dixon — shows a generic Democrat leading a generic Republican by 8 points, 49% to 41%. When we assign the leading candidates’ names to the question, both Craig and Flanagan lead Tafoya by around 7 points. This includes the Craig campaign’s own poll. 
When we say that everyday voters are starting to tune in, that means they’re being exposed to the seemingly neverending tidal wave of television and digital video ads, especially on the Democratic side. There are ads booked by Craig and Flanagan proper, and then there are even more ads paid for by outside money, such as North Star Dawn for Craig and the Democratic Lieutenant Governors Association for Flanagan, who was formerly a chair.
The only recent nonpartisan public polling with a head-to-head matchup on the Democratic column is by KSTP-TV, the ABC affiliate in the Twin Cities. Their polling by SurveyUSA showed a 5-point lead for Craig in mid-June and even support in mid-July. Looking at partisan polling — which is only ever published by choice — Craig and supporting PACs have Craig leading in half their polls, while Flanagan and supporting groups have Flanagan leading in all six polls since January, most recently a Public Policy Polling text poll that showed a 14-point lead for Flanagan.
Many Minnesota voters may be wondering where all the money for the endless cable and YouTube ads comes from. Over the two-year cycle through June 30, Craig has raised $10.5 million, while Flanagan has raised just under $6 million. Flanagan raised 45% of all dollars contributed from individual small-dollar donors; that is, donors who over the 18 months gave in total less than $200. By contrast, Craig raised 19% of dollars this way, where individual names are not required to be reported publicly.
Flanagan went into July with $1.6 million cash-on-hand. Craig, $5 million.
North Star Dawn has spent more than $11.9 million on television and digital advertising to benefit Craig. The DLGA has spent over $2.4 million on mailings and advertising to benefit Flanagan.
The Flanagan campaign is optimistic that the grassroots organizing that won her the DFL endorsement by a voice vote can win the primary on August 11; as her supporters say, “the many over the money.” 
For Craig, the primary ballot offers a fresh opportunity to expand the universe of potential voters, not just those who are willing to endure hours of caucuses and conventions with minimal air conditioning. Strong fundraising can get her message over the airwaves.
The poll that matters most is the one that is by a paper ballot. In Minnesota, the U.S. Senate contest is a partisan primary. There will be one Democrat and one Republican on the general election ballot, the winner of each primary. 
On the primary ballot, there is one paper sheet with two columns for each major party, but all voters are required to stick to one party and not switch over between columns. Which column a voter chooses and who they vote for are both secret. Well-informed voters may be strategic about which partisan primary column of the ballot they vote on, especially independently-minded voters.
Remember to make your voice heard and your vote count. Early voting is happening now. Primary day is Tuesday, Aug. 11.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: With House vote, Beacon Hill inches closer to landmark primary care reforms
description: Negotiations on a final compromise could prove arduous, but the House and Senate agree on the fundamental idea of more than doubling the share of health care spending that goes toward primary care to ease the crisis that’s left many patients struggle to find appointments.
text:
AFTER KEEPING onlookers guessing for weeks about the contours of its plan, the House made clear with a resounding vote Thursday that its leaders, too, want to force the Massachusetts health care industry to dedicate significantly more resources to a primary care sector in crisis.
Representatives embraced a sweeping bill that would more than double the share of health care spending that goes toward the front lines of care, plus erect new limitations around how insurers can use artificial intelligence and require more money from drug rebates to flow to patients.
Coming six weeks after a similar bill cleared the Senate, the House’s unanimous vote signals that lawmakers are ready to fashion a far-reaching bill that could fundamentally reshape the state’s health care landscape.
Wayne Altman, a family medicine physician in Arlington who has long been urging policymakers to improve support for primary care, said a final accord could become the most impactful health care legislation in Massachusetts since the reform package known as “Romneycare” was enacted two decades ago.
“Both of these bills are outstanding bills, and in and of themselves would be historic, national stories,” Altman said of the House and Senate proposals. “This primary care bill that will pass in 2026 will be a national model for primary care legislation all over the country in the same way Romneycare was for Obamacare.”
The hard work is not done. While both branches are in alignment on some of the biggest general ideas, legislative negotiators will now need to hash out a host of specific details and find common ground on areas where the House and Senate diverged. They have the next five months to do so before the legislative term ends.
Doctors, patients, and advocates have been warning for years that the primary care system is teetering in a precarious position. Physicians are leaving the field more quickly than new practitioners are joining, and securing an appointment has become increasingly difficult. One survey published in June 2025 found that a patient in the Boston area needed to wait an average of 69 days to book a physical with a new provider, the longest among 15 cities studied.
Primary care receives comparatively little investment. In 2024, primary care accounted for only about 6.6 percent of spending by commercial insurers, down from an even 7 percent a year earlier.
Both the House and Senate bills would force that figure upward, requiring at least 15 percent of health care expenses in Massachusetts to go toward primary care. That embraces one of the central recommendations from a task force that studied primary care problems, which counted Altman among its members.
Under the House bill, regulators will monitor health care entities for their compliance with new primary care spending requirements. Those that fail to devote enough dollars toward primary care can be required to file a plan detailing how they will come into compliance, and if they still fall short, they might be subject to a performance improvement plan — one of the main levers the state can use currently if a hospital or other actor is contributing to excessive health care spending growth.
Embracing a higher primary care spending floor is a full turn for Beacon Hill. Former governor Charlie Baker twice filed legislation that sought to boost dollars going to primary care, but neither of his proposals ever received a vote in the House or Senate, and Baker later reflected that his idea “freaked everyone out.”
The move could generate tension. If lawmakers conclude they want to increase the share of health care money that goes toward primary care, but avoid increasing overall health care spending, that means other segments such as pharmaceuticals or specialists might receive less of the pie — or at least smaller growth in future years — than they would under the status quo.
The House bill also calls on insurers to offer new payment models to primary care providers. Instead of defaulting to the current fee-for-service approach, in which practitioners are paid for each separate service or test, plans would have to make available a flat per-member per-month payment. Supporters argue that will make it easier for doctors to provide more comprehensive care because they can respond to patient needs without incurring additional administrative work of billing for multiple, discrete services.
Jennifer Lemmerman, executive director of the Health Care for All group, said the bill “will help patients access more timely, affordable primary care and begin to address the deep concerns about primary care access we hear from patients” every day.
There are several noteworthy areas of difference between the House and Senate bills that legislative negotiators will need to navigate.
The House version, but not the Senate bill, would prohibit insurers from using AI-powered automated tools as the “sole basis” to decide not to cover a procedure or service; those rulings would instead need to come from licensed health care professionals.
Lora Pellegrini, the head of the Massachusetts Association of Health Plans, called those proposed requirements “unnecessary.”
“State law already requires that adverse utilization review determinations be made by appropriately licensed clinicians, and the Division of Insurance has established comprehensive standards governing insurers’ responsible use of artificial intelligence,” Pellegrini said in a statement.
Another House addition calls on insurance carriers and the middlemen known as pharmacy benefit managers to pass along the majority of savings from prescription drug rebates to patients by limiting what they pay.
House Speaker Ron Mariano said his chamber’s approach also recognizes that different types of hospitals face different economic realities. “We make allowances for the different situations that different hospitals are in. Some are financially a little better off than others,” Mariano told reporters Thursday before the vote. “We make it fairer.”
One of the biggest areas of divergence is the timeline. The Senate bill seeks to reach the 15 percent primary care spending target within three years, while the House’s would ramp up to that point over the course of a decade.
That longer timeline is Altman’s chief concern with the House bill.
“Family physicians and primary care physicians are retiring early. They’re leaving the profession altogether. They’re reducing their hours. They’re leaving for concierge care,” Altman said. “We can’t wait until 2036.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Where do the candidates for governor stand on data centers?
description: Nearly 100 Monticello residents, decked out in red shirts, crowded into City Council chambers in February — nearly doubling the average attendance — holding signs protesting future data center development. The meeting stretched for nearly three hours, as residents interrupted debate between council members, calling for a moratorium on data centers. It’s a fa[...]
text:
Protest signs stand in a front yard near the land earmarked for a large data center campus in Hermantown, Minnesota, just outside of Duluth, is shown Friday, Oct. 24, 2025. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Nearly 100 Monticello residents, decked out in red shirts, crowded into City Council chambers in February — nearly doubling the average attendance — holding signs protesting future data center development.
The meeting stretched for nearly three hours, as residents interrupted debate between council members, calling for a moratorium on data centers.
It’s a familiar scene across Minnesota, in small communities and big cities, ruby red and indigo blue alike. 
A recent Star Tribune/Kare 11/Hubbard School of Journalism poll found that 63% of Minnesotans oppose data center construction in their communities. 
Among their concerns: air, noise and light pollution; the risk of increased electricity bills; and water consumption needed to cool down servers. 
Data centers have multiplied in Minnesota since 2010, storing your banking and medical records and cat videos, but so-called hyperscale data centers — housing the massive computing power necessary for AI — are attracting new and withering scrutiny. 
Minneapolis, Eagan, Elk River, Inver Grove Heights, Apple Valley and Rosemount have enacted moratoriums in last-minute attempts to delay data center construction amid residential outcry. But the tech giants are pressing on, saying Minnesota’s relatively cool climate, available land, electricity and water make it the ideal environment for development.
A data center owner recently sued Eagan over its one-year data center moratorium. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Amid that passionate and widespread opposition, Minnesota’s next governor will confront a significant policy and political challenge. 
Data center construction has delivered high-paying jobs for skilled tradespeople like electricians and plumbers. The data centers can also be a significant source of property tax revenue amid a volatile fiscal environment that’s forced metro cities in particular to enact big property tax hikes in recent years, which also anger residents. 
Thus far, data center development has played little role in the campaign to determine Minnesota’s next governor. 
The Reformer sent a questionnaire to the four major gubernatorial candidates ahead of the August 11 primary. We asked if they would approve additional tax incentives, as well as water and environmental permits. And, if they would allow local governments to pass temporary moratoriums, and to sign non-disclosure agreements with tech companies. 
GOP-endorsed candidate Kendall Qualls and Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth did not respond to multiple requests for comment. 
MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell
Lindell, the Trump-backed gubernatorial candidate, said he approves of data center construction that does not cater to “corporate welfare or secrecy deals that loot Minnesota’s resources for Big Tech cronies.”
At least eight Minnesota cities and two counties signed non-disclosure agreements with tech companies over prospective data center proposals, shrouding the negotiation process in secrecy through code names and confidential documents. 
Hermantown listed planning documents under the code name “Project Loon.” Rosemount, where Meta recently completed a data center project, hid Facebook’s parent company’s involvement under “Project Bigfoot.”
There was a bipartisan effort to ban local officials from signing NDAs with tech companies, but the bill stalled in the Legislature this year. 
Asked if he would support a similar ban, Lindell said yes. 
Want an AI data center in your city? Sure, but first sign this non-disclosure agreement.

Lindell said he would only approve additional water and environmental permits for data centers with protections in place for farmland.
“Strict scrutiny only — with full cost recovery, recycling mandates, and real protections for aquifers and farmland first,” Lindell said. 
Minnesota currently offers data centers sales tax exemptions if they exceed 25,000 square feet. New data centers must invest at least $30 million within four years, whereas refurbished data centers must invest at least $50 million in two years. 
“Repeal the exemptions,” Lindell said. “Taxpayers and ratepayers shouldn’t subsidize these grid- and water-straining operations.”
Lindell supports local governments enacting moratoriums on hyperscale data center projects, which house over 5,000 servers and span over 10,000 square feet, pending independent reviews that address “cumulative energy, water, land use and taxpayer costs.”  
“Minnesota’s future belongs to families, farmers, and producers — not server farms for out-of-state billionaires,” Lindell said. “We prioritize transparency, accountability and ending the two-tiered grift.”
U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar
Klobuchar, the presumptive Democratic nominee, did not respond directly to the Reformer‘s specific questions about local moratoriums or the use of NDAs in data center negotiations. 
“The Senator supports robust environmental standards for any proposed data centers as well as greater transparency and local control over decisions to build,” said Darwin Forsyth, Klobuchar’s spokesman. 
The Legislature passed a bill in 2025 requiring data centers to pay for the full cost of their energy usage, including equipment upgrades, to keep energy costs down for consumers. 
“That legislation was a good start, and the senator will work with legislators if additional changes are necessary to protect Minnesota consumers,” Forsyth said. “Her number one focus will be on protecting Minnesotans’ energy bills and our state’s water throughout the process.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Opponents sue state over Morris mega-dairy expansion
description: Food & Water Watch and the Land Stewardship Project sued the state of Minnesota Thursday over a decision to allow a Morris mega-dairy to expand without a more rigorous environmental review.  Riverview wants to expand West River Dairy from 7,855 cows to almost 19,000 cows, making it the biggest dairy in Minnesota.  The new dairy […]
text:
Riverview Dairy is seeking to expand their Morris-based West River Dairy operation from 7,855 cows to almost 19,000 cows. (Drone photo by Rob Levine/Minnesota Reformer)Food & Water Watch and the Land Stewardship Project sued the state of Minnesota Thursday over a decision to allow a Morris mega-dairy to expand without a more rigorous environmental review. 
Riverview wants to expand West River Dairy from 7,855 cows to almost 19,000 cows, making it the biggest dairy in Minnesota. 
The new dairy would create roughly the same amount of waste as a city of 750,000, and, according to the plaintiffs, at least 66,000 tons of additional greenhouse gas emissions yearly.
“It is hard to overstate the environmental destruction threatened by Riverview’s proposed West River factory farm expansion,” Food & Water Watch Legal Director Tarah Heinzen said in a press release. 
Riverview partner Brady Janzen said that the company would expand West River Dairy responsibly: “Our goal is to always be good neighbors, which includes protecting the environment and supporting the rural communities where we live and work,” he wrote in an email to the Reformer. 
The dairy plans to make use of all that waste by spreading it on nearby fields as fertilizer, for instance, Riverview says. 
The Minnesota Pollution Control Agency decided last month Riverview does not need to complete what’s known as an Environmental Impact Statement to move forward with the expansion. 
Opponents fear the impact of West River Dairy on local water quality, citing potential nitrate pollution; the dairy is next to the Pomme de Terre River and an unnamed creek. 
Fertilizer runoff can be a contaminant to drinking water, particularly in rural Minnesota where more people rely on private wells than in urban areas. 
Nearly 1 in 5 Americans’ drinking water contains elevated nitrate levels, which are linked to cancer and birth defects, according to Environmental Working Group. 
Matthew Sheets, an organizer with the Land Stewardship Project and a Morris resident, said in a statement that the decision forego the EIS “left so many questions unanswered. We deserve to know our community will be safe from any impacts this project will have.”
Before forgoing the EIS, the MPCA prepared and distributed a required Environmental Assessment Worksheet to analyze the potential impacts of the expansion. 
State law dictates that when reviewing an EAW, the MPCA must consider environmental effects’ type, extent, reversibility and ability to be controlled.  
After reviewing the document, the MPCA concluded that the expansion had no potential for significant economic impacts, and that no EIS was required. 
Food & Water Watch and the Land Stewardship Project said that MPCA’s analysis was deficient. Significant environmental impacts from the expansion “are not just possible, but likely,” the two groups wrote. Their petition requests judicial review of MPCA’s decision not to issue an EIS.
MPCA cannot comment on pending or ongoing litigation, said Daniel Strohl, a spokesman,. 
Beyond environmental concerns, opponents say the expansion will worsen the concentration of Minnesota’s dairy industry, endangering smaller family dairies that are already struggling to survive. 
“Consolidation is reshaping our dairy sector, and the trend has implications for land access, local economies and the next generation of farmers,” said Minnesota Farmers Union Vice President Anne Schwagerl in a press release last month.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania asks Trump administration how exactly it identified potential noncitizen voters
description: Pennsylvania state officials are pushing back on the Trump administration’s claim that there may be more than 14,000 potential noncitizens registered to vote in the state.
text:
Chester County election workers process ballots in West Chester, Pennsylvania, on Nov. 5, 2024. In 2025, a pollbook printing error resulted in thousands of voters being forced to cast provisional ballots. (Photo by Kriston Jae Bethel for Votebeat)This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access.
Pennsylvania state officials are pushing back on the Trump administration’s claim that there may be more than 14,000 potential noncitizens registered to vote in the state.
In a letter sent Wednesday to U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt said the federal government has not disclosed the methodology or data source it used to identify the noncitizens.
Schmidt also pointed out gaps in a program that the Department of Homeland Security uses to identify noncitizens.
“As you know, past analyses of voter lists have relied on faulty methodologies that can lead to inaccurate results and false claims about the citizenship status of eligible voters,” Schmidt wrote. “In fact, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services official who oversees [the program] has ‘acknowledged that the system can’t always find the most current citizenship information for people not born in the U.S.’”
Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt holds a press conference to provide an update on the administration of Pennsylvania’s primary election. (Commonwealth Media Services)
Earlier this month, President Donald Trump gave a primetime address in which he made several allegations of foreign election interference and issues with the nation’s voting systems. One of his claims was that the Department of Homeland Security had identified more than 250,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls of California, New Jersey, Nevada, and Pennsylvania.
In a letter to Schmidt the same day, Mullin wrote that a “preliminary review” had revealed “there may be as many as 14,576 non-citizens registered to vote in Pennsylvania.” A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania Department of State said Thursday that the federal government still has not shared the actual list of those people.
The Department of Homeland Security has not publicly disclosed, or disclosed to the other three states, precisely how it identified the potential noncitizen registrants. Letters to the states said the department used publicly available information but matched some of the potential noncitizens using Social Security numbers. All four states have refused to give the federal government versions of their voter rolls containing that information, saying state law prohibits them from disclosing it.
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Schmidt’s letter or a request for information on its methodology.
The system Schmidt was referring to — the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, program — has erroneously flagged some citizens as ineligible to vote. A judge recently blocked an overhaul of the program, citing in part the accuracy issues.
Dion Nissenbaum contributed reporting.
Carter Walker is a reporter for Votebeat in partnership with Spotlight PA. Contact Carter at cwalker@votebeat.org.

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye



Mocking Jim Jordan. Cleveland.com’s Sabrina Eaton reports, “Fauci diary reveals private mockery of Jim Jordan at COVID hearings.”
Anthony Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, repeatedly trashed U.S. Rep. Jim Jordan in a private diary released this week by Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul.
Entries from the diary’s 2020-2022 time frame describe the Champaign County Republican as “ranting” and mock his combative style at multiple hearings.


Afroman now files suit. The Cincinnati Enquirer’s David Ferrara reports, “Afroman files lawsuit against deputy in ‘Lemon Poundcake’ suit, raid.”
Rapper Afroman is suing a former deputy who previously sued him over music videos made from raid footage. The new lawsuit claims the deputy’s original suit defamed Afroman and invaded his privacy.
The deputy, Brian Newland, was part of a 2022 raid on Afroman’s home that resulted in no charges. Afroman previously won a lawsuit filed by Newland and other deputies over his music videos.


Lima billboard battle. The Columbus Dispatch’s Lilli Malone reports, “Anti-LGBTQ+ billboards in Lima prompt vocal community response.”
Anti-LGBTQ+ billboards have appeared in Lima, Ohio, and other cities, sponsored by an organization called Them Before Us. Community members and LGBTQ+ organizations have criticized the billboards for being harmful to children and families.
In response, local organizers planned a peaceful protest to promote a message of love and support for all family types. A GoFundMe campaign raised over $18,000 to launch counter-billboards with supportive messages across Ohio.


Ohio lynching sites. The Ohio Newsroom’s Kaitlin Thorne reports, ““This happened in our country and we can’t erase it.” A southeast Ohio museum displays soil from lynching sites.”
On a small shelf in an old brick building in Belmont County sit 14 jars of soil. Each is labeled with an Ohio city alongside a man’s name and contain dirt from sites across the state where the men were lynched.
The jars are on temporary display at the Underground Railroad Museum in Flushing, before the museum moves into its new home in Morristown, 8 miles down the road, this fall.

With the support of a tireless counselor (beautifully sincere Annette Deao), the brothers work toward a brighter, sober future.

title: Cortez Masto slams Trump immigration policies, and Biden’s too
description: Nevada Democratic U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto this week called President Trump’s immigration policies “extreme” and “un-American” and said former President Biden “placed too little emphasis on border security.” “I think I speak for everyone here when I say that we thoroughly understand the failures of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda,” Cort[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto at Center for American Progress event on July 29, 2026. (Photo courtesy Cortez Masto's office)Nevada Democratic U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto this week called President Trump’s immigration policies “extreme” and “un-American” and said former President Biden “placed too little emphasis on border security.”
“I think I speak for everyone here when I say that we thoroughly understand the failures of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda,” Cortez Masto said during a speech at a Center for American Progress event in Washington, D.C. Wednesday.
“Every day, we’re hearing about masked agents without identification coming into our neighborhoods with the intention of intimidating and attacking immigrants. ICE agents are attacking peaceful protestors and killing American citizens.” 
While Cortez Masto criticized the Trump administration, she said “the Biden administration did not handle immigration policy well either.” 
The Biden administration placed “too much emphasis on supporting the newly arriving asylum seekers,” she said, and overlooked undocumented immigrants who lived in the United States for decades.
Cortez Masto this week reintroduced the Fairness for Immigrant Families Act, which failed to pass in 2021. The bill would eliminate three- and 1o- year immigration bars, which block undocumented immigrants from reentering the United States after they leave or get deported for three or 10 years after residing in the country without legal status. 
Cortez Masto said the bill would reestablish the 245 (i) program, which allows undocumented immigrants to adjust their legal status by paying a penalty fee and is only eligible for those who filed for the program on or before April 30, 2001. The bill also promises to protect DACA recipients, parents of U.S. citizen children, and immigrants with pending applications from deportation, and crack down on fraudulent immigration services.
“The legislation pulls down some of the arbitrary barriers in our current immigration laws that keep people undocumented with no way of fixing their status,” she said. “It protects immigrant families from fraud. And it’s been updated to address the new threats we’re seeing under the second Trump administration.” 
Cortez Masto described her proposal as a way for the nation to learn from past mistakes and “offer pragmatic solutions to our country’s broken immigration system.”
But, with a Republican majority in the Senate and Trump still in office, the bill is not likely to pass. 
Cortez Masto did not directly condemn ICE in her comments, but she acknowledged the community fear surrounding the organization, stating detainment based on physical appearance “erodes all Americans’ civil liberties.” 
Cortez Masto also commented on the current administration’s intentional delay of DACA renewals and the fear immigrant families face daily, calling it “horrific” and “unacceptable.” 
Along with the emotional factors, she highlighted the positive economic impact of immigrants. Undocumented immigrants contributed over $37 billion in state and local taxes in 2022, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. In Nevada, undocumented immigrants accounted for over $500 million of that amount.

name: Nevada Current
title: Medicare & Medicaid’s 61st birthday not so happy thanks to Trump’s big bill, advocates warn
description: For 55-year-old Ivon Meneses, Medicaid has become a lifeline to afford treatments for her myriad of health problems including asthma and diabetes, which has come with a slew of medical complications for her.  The federally funded program, which was first signed into law 61 years ago as of Thursday, has been a safety net for […]
text:
Ivon Meneses speaking during a press conference in Las Vegas Thursday. (Photo courtesy Battle Born Progress)For 55-year-old Ivon Meneses, Medicaid has become a lifeline to afford treatments for her myriad of health problems including asthma and diabetes, which has come with a slew of medical complications for her. 
The federally funded program, which was first signed into law 61 years ago as of Thursday, has been a safety net for Meneses and many others who wouldn’t be able to pay for health care. 
“This program is not just a line item in the federal budget,” Meneses said. “It is absolutely the foundation to my daily survival. Medical coverage isn’t an option for me.”
Members of Battle Born Progress, Nevada Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, and SEIU 1107 gathered Thursday to condemn cuts to Medicaid as a result of Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
An estimated 70,000 Nevadans will lose medical coverage due to federal rule changes and spending cuts under the legislation, said Shelbie Swartz, executive director of Battle Born Progress, referencing the Nevada Medicaid administrator’s presentation to state legislators earlier this year.
“This isn’t an abstract policy,” Swartz said. “It’s a grandmother rationing insulin, it’s a mother watching her son’s disability coverage hang by a thread, it’s a rural clinic deciding whether it can keep its doors open.”
Health care providers and state legislators have been among those warning about the challenges ahead in Nevada next year when most of the Medicaid cuts in the Trump bill take effect.
Those challenges will likely be compounded as a result of the Trump administration announcing this week it was ending a subsidy designed to help Medicare recipients with out of pocket expenses. 
Of the many provisions of the climate, health care and tax law signed by President Joe Biden in 2022, known as the Inflation Reduction Act, capped out of pocket costs of the Medicare Part D prescription drug benefit at $2,000.
Nearly 470,000 Nevadans were enrolled in Medicare Part D in 2025, according to a KFF analysis.
All the changes and disruptions to access to health care show that “Republicans are doubling down on putting profits over people and making it harder for people to get health care,” Meneses said. 
Prior to being an organizer for Mi Familie Vota, Meneses worked as a casino porter and was able to get her health care costs covered through employment-related insurance. 
In an interview, she said health complications stemming from diabetes have left her disabled and unable to work full time. 
Like many working people who have trouble finding health insurance coverage, she turned to Medicaid. 
“Latinos are workers and we’ve given so much to this country,” she said during the press conference. “Unfortunately we know that Latinos are overrepresented in industries that do not offer employer-sponsored health insurance. We cannot afford any cuts to these critical important programs.”
The State of Nevada, Tesla, Walmart, and Amazon are among the state’s employers with the most Medicaid recipients, according to a 2026 report.
Meneses said it has become increasingly hard for her to walk, further cutting into her ability to work. As her vision began to fail, she also had surgery on her eyes last month.  
Without Medicaid coverage to pay for numerous prescriptions and procedures, “I would face impossible choices paying for housing and getting health care,” Meneses said.
Access to Medicaid for people like Meneses is going to become even more challenging. 
A new work requirement authorized under the Big Beautiful Bill and scheduled to start Jan. 1, 2027 will require adults to prove they are working, going to school, or volunteering for at least 80 hours a month to maintain their coverage.
The new rule applies to people aged 19-64 who gain Medicaid coverage through the Affordable Care Act expansion. Beneficiaries will also have to reapply every six months instead of once a year. 
An estimated 280,000 Nevadans who benefited from expanded Medicaid coverage are expected to be affected by the change. 
The rule is supposed to exempt those deemed “medically frail,” which could include pregnant people, foster youth up to age 26, veterans with total disability, Native Americans, incarcerated people, those in treatment for drug or alcohol use disorder, but state health officials have warned determining eligibility will be extremely complex.
Meneses said she has spoken to a social worker about the new requirements and was told she could also volunteer in lieu of finding work. But even that seems daunting as Meneses struggles to walk. 
“I fear I won’t be able to work because my complications are getting worse and worse and worse,” she said. “It’s scary. I still have a teen who is only 13. Imagine losing my vision. Who is going to take care of her?”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: BMW battery plant nears completion in Upstate SC
description: BMW will begin assembling battery packs for its new, South Carolina-built electric vehicles in December.
text:
BMW will begin assembling battery packs  at its Woodruff battery plant in December 2026 for its new, South Carolina-built electric vehicles. (Photo courtesy of BWM)WOODRUFF — BMW will begin assembling battery packs for its new, South Carolina-built electric vehicles in December.
The German automaker has already hired and begun training more than 300 people at the battery assembly plant near the town of Woodruff, 15 miles from its vehicle plant in nearby Greer.
Those employees will work alongside 250 robots to put together the batteries for the all-electric iX5, which the company unveiled in June.

BMW will begin assembling battery packs at its Woodruff battery plant in December 2026 for its new, South Carolina-built electric vehicles. (Photo courtesy of BWM)

BMW, in 2022, announced its electric vehicle plans for its Upstate South Carolina plant.
It has since invested $1.7 billion into both the existing, 10 million-square-foot factory in Greer, as well as a new, 1-million-square-foot, battery assembly plant on 314 acres in Woodruff.
In exchange for that investment, the state offered up a $52 million grant to purchase the land in Woodruff and pay for offsite environmental improvements to offset the loss of acreage to development, as well as grade the property, which BMW officials said used to be home to a peach farm, to get it ready for construction.
The company also received income tax credits for each of the roughly 300 new jobs, according to the state Department of Commerce. Those credits are worth $1,500 for each new job.
At the same time, BMW announced it would partner with Envision Automotive Energy Supply Co. (AESC), a Japanese-headquartered company, to make the cells for the battery packs.
Last year, however, AESC pressed pause indefinitely on its $1.6 billion battery cell plant under construction near Florence.
Electric vehicle battery company halts construction of SC manufacturing plant

AESC representatives said then that the company “fully intends to meet our commitments to invest $1.6 billion and create 1,600 jobs in the coming years,” but did not indicate what the new timeline might be.
Neither the company nor Florence County economic development officials responded to messages from the SC Daily Gazette about an updated restart.
In the meantime, AESC is expected to ship battery cells made in its China facilities to the BMW battery plant in Woodruff, said Rich Everly, vice president of production at BMW Group Plant Woodruff.
Inside the Woodruff plant, employees are getting ready for the start of production by training on a virtual reality platform that mimics the assembly work they’ll be doing on the production line.
And on a sneak peak tour of the plant last month, reporters from the SC Daily Gazette and other news outlets got a glimpse of how the factory will operate.
At the start of the assembly line, thousands of cylindrical battery cells will be glued together in clusters, which will give the iX5 the capacity to drive 435 miles per charge.
BMW workers train on virtual reality stations at the company's Woodruff battery plant, preparing for production to start in December 2026. (Photo courtesy of BWM)BMW workers train on virtual reality stations at the company's Woodruff battery plant, preparing for production to start in December 2026. (Photo courtesy of BWM)BMW workers train on virtual reality stations at the company's Woodruff battery plant, preparing for production to start in December 2026. (Photo courtesy of BWM)BMW workers train on virtual reality stations at the company's Woodruff battery plant, preparing for production to start in December 2026. (Photo courtesy of BWM)
From there, the cell clusters are transferred to the next set of stations, where they’re cleaned by lasers, welded by robots and inspected using camera and artificial intelligence systems.
“In Woodruff, we are combining cutting-edge processes, artificial intelligence and the expertise of our employees to create a production facility designed for the highest quality,” Raymond Wittman, a member of the Board of Management at BMW, said in a statement.
The clusters are then sealed inside a foam-filled battery pack, roughly the size of a queen mattress.
Thousands of cylindrical batter cells will be glued into clusters at BMW’s Woodruff battery plant to make packs for the company’s new, South Carolina-built electric vehicles. (Photo courtesy of BWM)
Some 50 trucks a day will enter and exit the Woodruff plant, Everly said, delivering supplies and sending finished battery packs to Greer to be installed in hybrid and all-electric vehicles.
The new iX5 will hit the market in early 2027, according to a June news release from the company.
The Greer vehicle plant, BMW’s largest in the world, produced more than 412,800 vehicles last year. Of those, around 200,000 were exported — a total value of $9 billion.
BMW has the capacity to make as many as 450,000 vehicles in Greer annually, Everly said, and updates to the plant allow it to shift seamlessly between gas, electric and hybrid vehicle production.
The Woodruff plant and Greer updates bring BMW’s total investment in South Carolina since 1992 to nearly $16 billion.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri voters weigh ending income tax. Here’s how other states replace the revenue
description: Voters have the opportunity Aug. 4 to put Missouri on track to be the 10th state without an individual income tax. Many of the states without an income tax have to get creative in the way they generate revenue to fund state operations. From property taxes and sales taxes to communication taxes and live entertainment […]
text:
(Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight).Voters have the opportunity Aug. 4 to put Missouri on track to be the 10th state without an individual income tax.
Many of the states without an income tax have to get creative in the way they generate revenue to fund state operations. From property taxes and sales taxes to communication taxes and live entertainment fees, revenue from these taxes is vital for providing essential services.
Individual income tax revenue made up 63% of the state’s general revenue in fiscal year 2025. The amendment asks voters to require the legislature to gradually reduce the individual income tax rate with the goal of eliminating it by 2032.
A yes vote will allow a broad sales tax on all goods and services to make up for the loss in revenue. This would repeal limits currently in place on such taxation. The state’s sales tax is 4.225%.
Gov. Mike Kehoe has suggested exemptions for healthcare, agriculture and real estate; the legislation passed by the House included no language for such exemptions.
The resolution’s sponsor, state Rep. Bishop Davidson, a Republican from Republic, noted the amendment that voters will consider does not mandate that the state make any changes to a sales tax. However, the Missouri budget must be balanced, so the loss in income tax revenue must be made up elsewhere.
Proponents of the resolution often compare Missouri to other states with no state income tax. Although a majority of these states rely on sales tax, their tax structures can vary drastically depending on different industries present, constitutional provisions or recent policy changes.
Here’s an overview of how the nine states without individual income tax generate state revenue:
Alaska became the first state to successfully repeal its income tax in 1980, thanks to the state’s oil boom. Almost all Alaskan oil production is on state-owned land, allowing the state to receive revenue in four different ways: production tax, property tax, royalties and corporate income tax.
According to the Resource Development Council, Alaska has made up to 90% of the state’s unrestricted general fund revenue from taxes related to oil in most years.
Roughly 30% of general fund revenue came from taxes on petroleum while 60% came from various investment returns. A majority of these investments came from Alaska’s permanent fund, which has received financial deposits used to invest in bonds, stocks and real estate.
Transfers from the fund make up a majority of investment revenues in Alaska’s unrestricted general and restricted designated general fund revenue.
Florida receives over 70% of its general revenue from sales tax with another 11% coming from corporate income tax. The state gets revenue from tourism through the Tourist Development Tax.
Nevada receives roughly 37% of its general revenue from a sales tax and use tax, including taxes on gaming fees, insurance premiums and a live entertainment tax.
The state’s base rate is 6.85%.
If Nevada were its own country, it would rank 10th in gold production, but tax revenue from natural resources only produces a small portion of revenue in taxes related to its natural resources. A state constitutional provision limits taxes on minerals.
New Hampshire phased out its individual income tax in 2025 and does not have a state sales tax either.
The state derives a little over a third of its budget from a business profits tax. New Hampshire has a meals and rooms tax, which serves as a form of tourism tax. This accounts for a little over one-tenth of its revenue.
New Hampshire makes up the remainder of its revenue from miscellaneous fees, such as its tobacco tax, Medicaid enhancement tax and its tax on real estate transfers.
South Dakota makes over 60% of its revenue from sales tax. The state has a base rate of 4.2% on general sales. The state also imposes a contractor’s excise tax, which is a 2% fee on the total cost of a construction project. This tax accounts for a little under one-tenth of the state’s budget.
Similar to Nevada, South Dakota has a strong mining industry but derives less than 1% of its revenue from its severance tax.
Tennessee makes up 60% of the state’s revenue from a general sales tax. Tennessee’s state sales tax is 7%. Tennessee employs a franchise and excise tax on corporations and businesses that contributes 16% of revenue.
In Texas, a 6.25% state sales and use tax is imposed on all retail sales, leases and rentals for most goods and certain services. The state first imposed a sales tax structure in 1961, and it provides over half of the state’s budget.
Texas fills the remainder of its budget with various taxes on motor vehicle sales, franchise taxes and taxes on the state’s natural resources.
Washington brings in about 45% of its budget from its sales and use tax. The state levies a fee of 6.5% on sales and transactions.
Washington makes almost a fifth of its budget from the state’s business and occupation tax, calculated based on the gross income of a business. The rate depends on which category of activity the business is classified as, with Washington having over 50 different classifications.
Washington also has a property tax that generates 13.4% of its revenue.
A massive reform to the state’s tax structure was approved in March when Senate Bill 6346 was signed into law: the first-ever “Millionaires Tax.” Beginning in 2028, a 9.9% income tax will be applied to taxable earnings above the $1 million standard deduction.
Wyoming makes a little under 40% of its revenue from its general and select sales tax structure.
Wyoming generates significant revenue from its mining industry. The state levies fees ranging from 1% to 6% for the various minerals and resources that are extracted.
Similar to Alaska’s permanent fund, the Permanent Wyoming Mineral Trust Fund receives revenue from its severance tax and is used by the state legislature to invest in various assets.
Investment income and severance taxes account for 47.51% of its general fund revenue, with miscellaneous revenue and tax sources filling the remainder of the budget.
Wyoming ranked ninth nationally for natural gas production and eighth in crude oil production in 2023. This allows the state to fund its entire budget reserve account just with federal mineral royalties or severance tax revenue.
State Rep. Steve Butz, a Democrat from St. Louis, argued that Missouri cannot replicate the similar success seen by other states that never had an income tax or repealed it.
“God bless Branson, but it’s not Orlando,” Butz said in a March committee hearing. “We are never going to be Texas, Texas has a huge percent of this nation’s energy in that state, and it’s just not below our ground.”
“You have to face the facts,” Butz added. “Tennessee hasn’t had an income tax; it’s not part of the way they fund their government, but their sales tax is dramatically higher.”
This story originally appeared in the Columbia Missourian. It can be republished in print or online.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Kratom alkaloids found in cat’s claw tablets linked to multiple overdoses, Utah agencies warn
description: A product labeled as cat’s claw is being removed from Utah shelves as Utah officials investigate a recent death and several severe health incidents that may be linked to it.  According to the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food and the Utah Poison Control Center, multiple flavors of Buzzers’ cat’s claw tablets were found to […]
text:
Buzzers Cat's Claw tablet packets. (Photo courtesy of Utah Department of Agriculture and Food)A product labeled as cat’s claw is being removed from Utah shelves as Utah officials investigate a recent death and several severe health incidents that may be linked to it. 
According to the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food and the Utah Poison Control Center, multiple flavors of Buzzers’ cat’s claw tablets were found to contain kratom alkaloids, a recently mostly-banned substance in the state. Additional details were not provided about the fatal overdose.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The agencies said in a new release they “warn all members of the public not to buy or consume Buzzers Cat’s Claw tablets and to safely destroy any existing product. Retailers should immediately remove products and contact UDAF’s Specialized Products Division.”
Cat’s claw, a woody vine, is considered to be a safe supplement promoted to treat joint pain and other conditions, so the Poison Control Center wouldn’t expect it to have opioid-like effects, said Amberly Johnson, director of the center. However, within the past several weeks, many calls made to the center have been related to cat’s claw tablets.
“Within 2026, we received around 40 calls related to kratom or kratom derivative products,” Johnson said, mentioning alkaloids like 7-OH, which occur naturally in kratom products but are often enhanced in labs. “Just within the past several weeks, we’ve seen an increase in about 19% of those cases have been related to these cat’s claw products that we suspected had a synthetic kratom derivative in them.”



Let us know what you think...


 


The state’s Department of Agriculture and Food confirmed those suspicions when officers tested the Buzzers products identified in overdose cases in recent weeks and found they contained mitragynine pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15, two opioid-acting compounds derived from the kratom plant, the agency said. 
The compounds, Johnson said, can be more potent than morphine, and can have withdrawal effects among users.
“We’d expect to see profound sedation or drowsiness, sleepiness, leading to, like, coma. And then also to effects on breathing, so really slow, shallow breathing, even to the point of someone not breathing,” Johnson said.
Johnson recommends administering naloxone in suspected overdoses from these products, and calling 911 to ask for medical help. Those with concerns about the substance’s adverse effects can also call the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222 anytime for free, expert advice.
