name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Are we losing our freedom of speech?
description: Everywhere I look, the concept of free speech is getting a workout. A food truck, a cake, a flag — all have stirred up emotions recently here in Indiana. Of course, the First Amendment applies only to freedom of speech as it pertains to government action. That’s why you hear people say, “freedom of speech doesn’t […]
text:
A protester carries a sign about free speech in Oregon. (Photo by Mia Maldonado/Oregon Capital Chronicle)Everywhere I look, the concept of free speech is getting a workout. A food truck, a cake, a flag — all have stirred up emotions recently here in Indiana.
Of course, the First Amendment applies only to freedom of speech as it pertains to government action. That’s why you hear people say, “freedom of speech doesn’t mean freedom from consequences.”
But I’m tired of how society has become a game of gotcha. It’s practically a national pastime to drag people online and call for their firing over their opinion.
Even a food truck at the Statehouse market can’t have a little fun with a slogan without getting kicked out because the phrase offended someone’s fragile sensibilities.
The Smash Daddy’s Burgers, Fries, Etc. food truck had been showing up to the market for almost two years. On the side of the truck is the slogan, “you’ll love our meat in your mouth.”
Yes, it’s sexual innuendo. No different than “where’s the beef” was in the 1980s for Wendy’s. There’s a company that advertises fudge and candy in the most sophomoric way possible on billboards in Indiana but it hasn’t been stopped from operating.
But suddenly after someone complained — not in writing, by the way — the truck was told not to return by the Indiana State Personnel Department.
Talk about an overreaction. If you don’t want to eat there, then fine. But it was a place that always had a line and the complainers cost the truck’s owner thousands in revenue.
That’s where we are at as a society?
The food truck owner might have a legal case since the government was involved and the phrase doesn’t count as obscenity.
Calling for jobs
But that’s not the only free-speech issue popping up lately.
Let’s take about the cake. A comedian and guest lecturer at George Washington University in Washington, D.C., took a crass cake to U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham’s office offering “congratudolences” after his death. She also posted harsh criticism against Graham.
It was tacky and awful and, of course, I don’t approve. But now many people want her fired from her adjunct position at Indiana University teaching one law school course.
In a letter addressed to IU President Pamela Whitten and the dean of the university’s McKinney law school in Indianapolis, the IndyStar reported that Republican U.S. Reps. Marlin Stutzman and Mark Messmer said Elizabeth Booker Houston should be fired for comments they describe as “vile and cruel” and that violate the university’s handbook.
Heck, Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith went further and said IU should lose all its state funding.
This call is similar to what colleges and universities faced after Charlie Kirk was killed and some employees were outed for inappropriate comments. Ball State University did fire an employee over a social media post, but she sued and won a $225,000 settlement.
Some are angry that Ball State settled instead of buttressing the legal case for future firings.
And then we have Attorney General Todd Rokita, who continues to post photos and social media rants against teachers in Indiana and their classroom décor. One recently highlighted a Perry Meridian High School classroom that has signs supporting LGBTQ+ rights, Black Lives Matter and more.
Others pointed out the flags and decoration encouraged civility and love for one another.
Rokita provided no information in his tweet or on the Eyes on Education portal about the veracity of the photos. Perry Township Schools Superintendent Patrick Spray clarified to the Capital Chronicle that the photos are not recent. He said the teacher resigned last school year for reasons unrelated to the issue.
More importantly, he provided context about the photos, noting that the Black Lives Matter and Free Myanmar photos are of student art.
“That is a classroom that receives newcomers to the country, so primarily refugees … and they are allowed to represent their thoughts and feelings in the classroom,” he said. “Now, I will say that we have worked with our staff and talked about keeping political things out of the classroom, especially if they don’t adhere to the curriculum being taught. We’ve just told them it’s not worth the negative attention you may receive as an individual.”
Another day, another attack on freedom of speech. I miss the days when we worried more about our own lives than everyone else’s. I miss when we had tolerance for other viewpoints — even the distasteful ones.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: After losing SNAP benefits, some CT refugees are struggling to afford food
description: An estimated 1,745 refugees and asylum seekers are expected to lose SNAP in Connecticut, a DSS spokesperson said.
text:
Syrian natives Karam and Noor have spent long days this summer sitting in the respite of their small New Haven apartment, listening to the gentle buzz of the air conditioner and the hum of Karam’s dialysis machine.
Weakened by kidney failure, Karam is unable to work and is tethered 12 hours a day to the machine that cleans the toxins from his blood.
Noor, who does not speak English and has found it difficult to find work, has always taken pains to feed her husband and their children a healthy diet of fresh foods, often cooking dishes from their homeland. That’s gotten harder to do since the family lost its food stamps in December due to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, also known as H.R. 1, which ended access to the program for refugees and asylum-seekers.
But salty food is dangerous for Karam and the shelf-stable food carried by pantries they’ve come to rely on the last eight months is often high in sodium.
“There’s been a 180 degree change” in the conditions of their daily lives since the family stopped receiving help from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, Noor said through a translator. “Now we have to focus on the cost of everything and we can barely afford essentials.”
Karam and Noor are not the couples’ real names; they requested anonymity because they are in the process of applying for green cards and fear retribution in a time when the federal government has ramped up deportations of some groups, shut down some programs and ended funding for others that served immigrants.

From left to right, Maria Ramirez, Christion Gilbert, Elizabeth Johnston, and Ana Cardenas stand in the Integrated Refugee and Immigrant Services in New Haven. All four work in the food pantry organizing distributions, managing the warehouse, and distributing goods to guests.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

In Connecticut, SNAP enrollment has decreased by about 35,000 since December, much of that tied to new federal work requirements, according to officials at the state Department of Social Services. An estimated 1,745 refugees and asylum seekers are expected to lose SNAP in Connecticut, a DSS spokesperson said.
Connecticut has partially filled the gap for people who have lost SNAP, providing millions in assistance to food pantries, grants to the Department of Agriculture, and $300 grocery cards for people who have recently lost SNAP. IRIS has also been able to provide a bridge of four months of supplemental assistance to families. 
The new federal policy affecting refugee food assistance is a stark reversal from the previous era of resettlements, in which such newcomers were helped with every step of the process — from searching for employment to securing housing and public benefits — by resettlement groups and federal funding. Today, groups like New Haven-based Integrated Refugee and Immigrant Services, or IRIS, are focused on helping families secure the means of supporting themselves on an accelerated timeline, as supports like SNAP vanish and they must get the needed skills to quickly join the labor force.
“Everyone’s timeline for becoming self-sufficient and dependent on their own resources is largely dependent on the skills and resources they came to the country with,” said Daniel Pflueger, deputy director of stabilization services at IRIS. For people who arrive fluent in English, the route to finding stable employment is shorter, he said, while others may need to learn a new language or learn a trade. 
In addition to the rental assistance IRIS provided in the first year, families also have also historically been supported by both SNAP and Temporary Family Assistance, a program that provides cash to families under 55% of the poverty line for up to 36 months.
“Now without SNAP, that changes the whole framework where immediately there are hundreds or well over a thousand dollars in some cases that people don’t have,” Pflueger said.
Karam and Noor came to Connecticut two years ago with the help of the International Organization for Migration. They left Syria during the civil war and then lived in Jordan for a decade, before securing refugee status in the United States.

Kate Lee hands out corn to food pantry guests at IRIS in New Haven. Lee has volunteered with the organization for 20 years and lives in Guilford.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Though they are living in the U.S. legally, with humanitarian status, they also try to limit their time outside the apartment because they don’t want to risk coming into contact with Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, who have swept up many residents of their adopted city over the past year.
Noor said she learned in November 2025 that the family of eight would no longer receive more than $1,000 a month for groceries through SNAP. 
Though H.R. 1 ended the program for refugees beginning in December 2025, not all recipients lost the benefit at the same time, according to Pflueger.
“It’s only when a family would have, say, their next renewal, or there’s an updated family member or house address change, something that would require a DSS agent to to open up their case,” Pflueger said.
Much of the food Noor’s family eats comes from food pantries, like canned fruit, bags of beans and rice and limited fresh food, like cabbage, onions and potatoes.
A New Haven pantry run by IRIS sometimes offers Halal meats, but Noor said her family has mostly gone vegetarian since the cuts. They eat smaller meals earlier in the day with less variety and have replaced dinner with a late-day snack to get them through the night.
With limited financial resources, IRIS says they are focused on preparing families to survive on their own. 
“Is there an opportunity to get a second job? Is there a 17-year-old in the family who can work in the summer or part time in the school year? Is there anyone in the family who could really get to a better opportunity of getting employed if they got their English up to the next level?” Pflueger said are some of the questions they ask families.
Noor and Karam’s six children are in school, ranging from young adults studying in college to her youngest who is three. As the mother of teenagers, it can be especially challenging to stretch their food.
“When I cook a big meal, I expect leftovers the next day, but it’ll be completely gone from the fridge,” she said through a translator.

From Left to right, Barbara Shiller, Eleanor Weseloh and Elizabeth Johnston organize food on the choice table. The table is stocked with fresh produce and prepared foods from Trader Joes.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

The family will also lose access to HUSKY, Connecticut’s Medicaid program, later this year. But Karam, who is currently on the state plan, should still be covered under a federal program for people with life-threatening conditions. Advocates say that for a family such as theirs, stress is coming from every angle. 
“Immigration enforcement is happening on a weekly basis, and when new policies come out, it is coupled with food insecurity for the population that we serve, it’s taking a toll on them,” said Mohammed Daad Serweri, associate director of resettlement services at IRIS. “It’s not only not having food — actual food on the table for the children to really have enough to eat— but it’s also the mental health and has really negatively impacted many of these parents.”
Families worry not only about how and where they will get enough food, but also whether it’s safe to visit a pantry because ICE could be present or how to schedule a job around pantry hours. “A lot of folks are making choices of what not to pay,” Pfleuger said. “So people are not paying their full rent, or people are skipping out on their utility bills so that they can buy food in the meantime.”
Many are hoping that they will be able to find a job to get back on track with those bills or that a green card application will go through, but currently “extraordinarily few” of those applications are being processed, according to Pflueger. A new policy allows immigration officers to hold the use of public assistance programs like SNAP and housing vouchers against green card applicants.
As they are confined to eating the foods they are given at pantries, families also lose access to the ingredients that help them summon the flavors of home. 
It’s now been eight months since Noor and Karam lost SNAP. They have received some assistance for their school-age children for the summer months through the SUN Bucks program — $120 per child — which has allowed Noor to buy healthy foods, and sometimes get her kids’ favorite snacks. 
Back in Syria, before he got sick, Karam was a farmer. Though there were other struggles, having enough to eat was never among them.
But difficult as the situation may be, the family is still glad to be here. 
“For my kids to be able to get an education at university level, I still see the benefits and I’m not really focusing on the drawbacks,” Noor said.

name: New York Focus
title: A Push to Accelerate Kids’ Asylum Cases Will Hasten Deportations, Attorneys Fear
description: The Trump administration has scheduled a flurry of asylum interviews, leaving children and attorneys scrambling to prepare.
text: Immigrant children who crossed the border into the United States without their parents to seek asylum are facing a barrage of changes that threaten to increase their odds of being deported. / Graphics: SR Raju / Pexels; xoxostd / Canva | Illustration: Leor Stylar

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Mailers aim to sway us on Kansas Supreme Court amendment, but mostly they deserve the dust bin
description: I messaged my friends and family this week asking for political mailers that they received. The replies that I got were nearly identical:  I think I tossed them. I trash them as they come in. They went out with the recycling yesterday. Ha. I just trashed/destroyed them last night. Maybe “destroyed” is a bit harsh, […]
text:
Kansans have been swamped by mailers about the judicial selection amendment on the ballot Aug. 4. (Photo by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)I messaged my friends and family this week asking for political mailers that they received. The replies that I got were nearly identical: 
I think I tossed them.
I trash them as they come in.
They went out with the recycling yesterday.
Ha. I just trashed/destroyed them last night.
Maybe “destroyed” is a bit harsh, but it’s the same in our house. Most political mailers addressed to us don’t even make it in the house from the mailbox — they go straight into the garage recycling bin.
For that reason, it’s interesting to see how Kansas campaigns try to reach voters when we see each slick cardstock design as junk mail. Our culture’s attention span to media messages gets shorter each year, so the design, imagery and words on political mailers must cut right to the point.
Along with a mixed bag related to candidate elections, my neighbors and I mostly receive mailers related to the amendment that would establish direct elections of Kansas Supreme Court justices. The message here is even simpler than a candidate election, where voters need to remember a name.
Here, as the mailers make clear, it’s just “yes” (establish elections) or “no” (maintain the current process). 
What did I see? Blunt messaging and simple images, aimed at catching our reluctant gaze and quickly persuading us.
 
Vote yes
The mailers for “yes” come with conservative messaging from political action committees such as the Prairie Fire PAC, connected with Attorney General Kris Kobach, and Americans for Prosperity, founded by the Koch brothers of Wichita.

Two recent “yes” mailers borrow the look of official government mailings. One of them combines a warning symbol, the words “IMPORTANT NOTICE” and a yellow warning to “DO NOT DISCARD.” Using an aesthetic that looks like it came from the local government (which is to say it’s hammerhead ugly) is a clever tactical twist, making the mailer stand out from the polished noise of the PACs. 
The look also associates the message of “VOTE YES” with a mailing that could come from the election office. One mailer provides early voting locations as the county board of elections might do. 

Designers further connect the “yes” campaign with civic responsibility by emphasizing the image of “I Voted” stickers. One mailing shows folks with the stickers on their chests, pointing to them in case we missed it. The image of a circular button dominates another mailing. 
The words of the “yes” campaign go even further, branding the decision as the “RIGHT TO VOTE AMENDMENT,” suggesting that we “LET THE VOTERS DECIDE.” 
You might, like me, see hypocrisy in conservative voices celebrating the right to vote as they simultaneously work to suppress voting in many other ways. Nevertheless, it’s a patriotic, wholesome and effective association. Even if it doesn’t address the deeper issue actually on the ballot, how do you dispute the virtue of voting?
All of this seems legitimate if not clever political messaging on behalf of PACs pushing voters toward yes. 

However, a pair of Americans for Prosperity Kansas mailings dip into the political muck in encouraging “yes” votes. My neighbor received a mailing promising three “FACTS” about the amendment. Instead, the mailing delivers partisan rhetoric such as, “The Kansas Supreme Court has been too soft on crime!” and “The ones controlling the court are lying to you.” 
So much for facts.
The biggest fumble came from a mailing that boldly centers all-caps text on a yellow background: “YOU DESERVE THE RIGHT.” There’s more than one way to read that.

One option? “You deserve the power to use the ballot box to vote for the Supreme Court in Kansas” aligns with their campaign. However, I also read it as being about being stuck in Kansas with conservative politicians at the helm, as in “You deserve the disastrous politics of rightwing politicians, since you voted for them, you Kansas dummies.”
The second meaning seems like a tough appeal, especially to Johnson County voters who are gradually shifting away from the Republican Party.
Both of the Americans For Prosperity Kansas mailers use a blue-and-yellow color scheme, which conjures the color scheme of the state flag. Another association might be politically familiar if you were in Kansas during the 2022 vote related to abortion rights. In that election, PACs that wanted us to vote no (a progressive vote to protect abortion rights) used blue and yellow on their yard signs. 
Not to mention, during the last few months, signs dotting the yards and medians of Johnson County use the same color scheme — but those ask us to vote “no.”
Using the blue-and-yellow palette here for the “yes” campaign might be an effort to sway (if not confuse) moderate or progressive voters. Maybe it’s just the state flag. 
Finally, from all of the “yes” mailings, my nomination for the most effective distillation of why to vote yes: “Only Kansas has an oddball system where lawyers, not voters, choose the judges.” That single line does so much — targeting the novelty of the current system, playing on cultural distrust of lawyers and pointing to voters being robbed of their power. 
 
Vote no
Unsurprisingly, the mailers for vote “no” used quite different techniques. 
Of the six mailers that I collected, the most common approach was a two-step: an appeal to expertise while using Kobach as an adversary. Each of these mailers was sent by Kansas United for Impartial Courts, chaired by Micah Kubic, who also works as executive director of the ACLU of Kansas. 

Mailers presented a few different authorities, including former Kansas Supreme Court Chief Justice Lawton Nuss (“I’m voting NO because our Supreme Court is NOT FOR SALE.”) and OB/GYN physician Selina Sandoval — a mailing that connected a vote against the amendment with the protection of abortion rights. 
With these authority figures staring solemnly into the camera, the vote appears grave — especially when paired with a somber, black background for the text. 
From the same group, I received a similarly designed mailer with a woman from Lawrence quoted as saying, “We already decided this.” It’s a nod to the 2022 vote on the “Value Them Both” abortion amendment. 
More broadly, those words play on our collective fatigue with politics, politicians and their games. The mailer rolls its eyes that conservatives in Kansas can’t get the message. Those words can also be read as voicing frustration about President Donald Trump, whose election denialism in 2020, was the ultimate political example of “we already decided this.”
None of the vote “no” messaging portrays hope. Instead, the mailers are mired in disorganization, negativity and opposition. 
One folded mailer promises, “HERE’S THE TRUTH,” but then delivers a buckshot pattern of all-caps, bold-faced and underlined assertions that don’t cohere around a central political idea. The random visuals include a handshake, people voting and shoes striding across a textured floor. What are voters to summon from that? 
Just how little positivity is in the mailers for the vote “no” effort? Take this quiz for me. 
Taken from a no-frills, black-and-white mailer from the same PAC, one set of verbs below describes what will happen if you vote “yes.” The other describes the effects of voting “no.” See if you can tell which is which. 
List #1: replaces / enables / makes it easier / increases
List #2: retains / shields / continues / keeps
The first list is clearly more positive — yet, it describes the vote “yes” initiative. Those word choices portray action and progress, while the second list is verbal molasses, appealing to tradition, if not intransigence. It’s baffling that these are the words that the PAC used to frame the choices in their own mailer. 

Kansas United for Impartial Courts found a more effective message and design with a vertical mailer showing a full-bleed photo of Kobach’s face obscured by text reading: “SO NOW THEY’RE TRYING AGAIN.” Extra points to the graphic designer who found a way to allow one of Kobach’s eyes to peek creepily through the cluster of words.
It’s tempting to say that the PAC is painting Kobach as the bogeyman, but Kobach legitimately is the opposition here, since he leads a rival PAC supporting the amendment. He slides easily into the role of villain, encouraged by his deep unpopularity statewide. Voters who realistically could be persuaded to vote “no” likely don’t like Kobach, even before they open their mail.
The strongest expression of the vote “no” messaging? “This amendment is an attempt to take away our power and ban abortion.” It is more direct than some of the other confused language in vote “no” mailers.
We might believe that mailers aren’t significant, given our boredom, if not irritation, at receiving them. It’s also possible that with the election’s timing — a midterm, primary election — every voter swayed by the mailbox will matter. 
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana AG sues Merrillville, accusing town of blocking new ICE facility
description: Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita says Merrillville officials are "interfering" with land buys for a potential ICE facility in the town.
text:
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita backs an immigration bill on Thursday, Feb. 19, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita on Wednesday filed suit against a northwest Indiana town he says is interfering with federal immigration enforcement efforts to add a new detention facility there.
Merrillville, Rokita said in a news release, is “effectively aid(ing) and abet(ing)” criminals.
As President Donald Trump’s administration ramps up its mass deportation scheme, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been on the hunt for more immigrant detainee holding space.
ICE has been trying to buy property in Merrillville, Rokita confirmed.
He’s accusing town leaders of discouraging or even thwarting ICE real estate transactions with property owners, in violation of state laws requiring local government cooperation with ICE.
The Office of Attorney General didn’t immediately provide a copy of the complaint, and it was not available on the state’s MyCase platform.
The lawsuit comes about a month after Rokita’s office issued Merrillville a cease-and-desist letter.
The letter told leaders to rescind a non-binding resolution opposing the conversion of warehouses into detention space, stop interfering in resident-ICE land deals, and issue a public statement clarifying that the town won’t oppose transactions or retaliate against any land owners who sell to ICE.
“We requested that Merrillville comply with state law and they refused, choosing instead to play games, effectively aid and abet criminal illegal aliens, and making the illegals’ evasion of justice a higher priority than the safety of taxpayers throughout the region,” Rokita said. “That’s illegal under Indiana law.”
Immigration crackdown heads to Indiana governor after falling short last year

Merrillville didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Officials have previously said their resolution is an expression of opinion protected by the First Amendment — not an enforceable policy — and noted they’re “oath-bound” to follow all state and federal laws.
The lawsuit represents the first enforcement action taken under a controversial new immigration enforcement law, according to Rokita’s office. Senate Enrolled Act 76 was approved in March.
Some provisions didn’t take effect until this month, but others were effective immediately — including authorizing Rokita to sue units of local government for up to $10,000 per violation of an existing ban on limiting immigration enforcement activities..
Local governments must also comply with ICE detainer requests.
The law additionally prohibits businesses from knowingly or intentionally employing unauthorized workers. Violators face escalating punishments ranging from operating authorization suspensions at one site to permanent revocations at all locations.
Rokita is sending video remarks to be played at a Saturday mass deportation rally headlined by former U.S. Border Patrol head Greg Bovino.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Uninsured but undaunted, a Portland surgical patient searched the globe for a deal
description: Around the end of last year, Ronmel Rangel, 63, began to feel a familiar discomfort in his lower abdomen. Twenty-five years earlier, while living in his native Venezuela, he had undergone surgery to repair a hernia on the right side of his groin. Now, the same pain had returned — on the left. This time, […]
text:
Uninsured and in need of hernia surgery, Ronmel Rangel collected estimates from facilities near and far from his home in Portland,
Maine, including some outside the United States. “I wasn’t going to mortgage my life just to have surgery and spend the next 30
years paying off the debt,” he says. (Photo by: Brianna Soukup /KFF Health News) 
This article first appeared on KFF Health News and is republished here under a Creative Commons License.

	Around the end of last year, Ronmel Rangel, 63, began to feel a familiar discomfort in his lower abdomen. Twenty-five years earlier, while living in his native Venezuela, he had undergone surgery to repair a hernia on the right side of his groin.
Now, the same pain had returned — on the left.
This time, Rangel was in the U.S. and lacked health insurance. In 2019, he moved to Portland, Maine, where one of his daughters lives.
As a green-card holder, he qualified to purchase health insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplace. But he quickly realized that the premiums for someone his age were beyond his budget. He decided to go without insurance, even though it had been a priority for him.
Instead, Rangel signed up for a plan at a concierge practice where patients pay as little as $70 a month for services, including unlimited office visits and minor procedures such as stitches and biopsies.
But when Rangel was diagnosed with a hernia, surgery became unavoidable. Ben Hagopian, his primary care physician, helped him compile a list of hospitals and surgical centers to consider. Rangel has a PhD in management, a field he pursued while serving in the navy in Venezuela. Armed with that knowledge and a naturally inquisitive mind, he began researching prices.
His efforts paid off when the bill came.
The medical service
Rangel had what is called an inguinal hernia, which occurs when the contents of the abdomen bulge through a weak spot in the lower abdominal wall. The condition is relatively common, particularly among older adults.
In most cases, surgery is required to fix the muscle wall and can be performed as an outpatient procedure. There are three main surgical approaches to repair an inguinal hernia: open, laparoscopic, and robot-assisted. Studies have shown that the three approaches have similarly low rates of hernia recurrence and are safe and effective.
Rangel underwent an open repair, an approach often preferred by physicians for recurrent hernias. He said his operation lasted less than two hours, and he walked out of the surgical center shortly afterward.
The bill
$2,900: The flat rate Rangel ultimately paid for his hernia repair at an outpatient surgery center in Maryland, including the surgeon’s fee and anesthesia. He said he also paid around $1,800 to travel to the surgery center from his home in Maine, including airfare, meals, and lodging for him and his wife.

The billing problem: No insurance — but time to shop
Because Rangel did not have insurance, he had no protections from high costs — except time and his ability to shop for an acceptable price for his procedure.
Rangel’s first stop was a nonprofit hospital close to home. He scheduled a consultation with a surgeon with MaineHealth, the state’s largest health system, and received an estimate showing it would cost approximately $23,000 to repair his hernia laparoscopically.
Laparoscopic procedures generally cost more because surgeons use more advanced tools. Still, the average laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair costs nearly twice as much at a hospital as it does at an ambulatory surgery center for a patient covered by Medicare, which pays $5,280 for the hospital-based option.
“I wasn’t going to mortgage my life just to have surgery and spend the next 30 years paying off the debt,” said Rangel, now 64.
So, he kept shopping. He considered a surgical center in Oklahoma that was far cheaper, but he ultimately ruled it out because it was so far away. He also explored traveling to Universidad de los Andes in Santiago, Chile, where another of his daughters lives. There, his hernia repair would have cost about $7,000, but once he added thousands of dollars in travel expenses, that option no longer made financial sense.
Gerard Anderson, a professor who analyzes healthcare spending at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, said patients without health insurance are often the ones hit hardest by wide price variations.
A closer look at any hospital bill helps explain why. “Every hospital is different,” he said, “but generally about half of the total charge is the facility fee,” a charge added to hospital care to help cover overhead costs.
Anderson said hospitals often mark up prices far more than smaller facilities do.
Medical billing researchers say the price gap between hospitals and ambulatory surgery centers partially reflects the higher overhead costs of operating a hospital.
Hagopian, Rangel’s physician, acknowledged that hospitals have higher administrative expenses. “But that doesn’t explain the high costs.”
MaineHealth declined to comment to KFF Health News, directing questions about the hospital-based procedure’s cost to Jeffrey Austin, president of the Maine Hospital Association.
Austin said that, unlike surgery centers, hospitals must absorb the costs of providing “money-losing” services, such as behavioral healthcare and care for Medicaid patients. He added that revenue generated by large hospitals in a health system supports other facilities, improving access to care.
Hospital prices, which can vary widely, are also driven by negotiations with insurers and market concentration. For uninsured patients, those list prices can become the starting point for negotiations — or the full amount owed.
Anderson noted that standardized payment rates exist for Medicare and Medicaid but not for most privately priced medical services. “In the private sector, providers can charge whatever they want.”

The resolution
Rangel has another daughter in Argentina, a son in Venezuela, and other family in Spain. But he decided to stop looking around the globe for a good price, because he finally found what he was looking for in Maryland.
In April, he traveled to the Affordable Hernia Surgery center in Rockville, where he said “an efficient, well-coordinated system” guided him through the entire process.
“I received professional and very human care,” Rangel said. He was fully recovered within two weeks, as his surgeon predicted, he said.
The surgery center charged Rangel a flat fee for his hernia repair. The added travel expenses for the two-day trip with his wife went toward airline tickets, transportation, meals, and one night in a hotel.
Rangel said he paid about $4,700 total.
Alan Kravitz, the surgeon who performed Rangel’s operation, said the price difference uninsured patients face compared with insured patients is far from fair. “In the predatory and strategic world of U.S. healthcare pricing, uninsured patients generally get charged more than providers would accept from Medicare or commercial insurance.”
Kravitz then pulled out an estimate another patient had received for an inguinal hernia repair from a different large health system. The price: $37,000.
The takeaway
Without insurance, many patients are on their own to negotiate.
“With the help of their primary physicians, patients can dig into prices and compare their options to avoid falling into medical debt,” Rangel said.
That approach, however, is most feasible for elective procedures with several surgical options offering comparable outcomes.
Patients facing medical emergencies do not have the luxury of comparing prices before seeking care, though many hospitals offer cash-pay discounts or charity care for those paying without insurance.
Billing analysts say patients who do have time to shop should look beyond cost alone. They recommend checking the quality of hospitals and surgical centers by reviewing publicly available ratings and patient reviews. Research has found that higher prices do not necessarily translate into a better quality of care, but it’s also important to select a reputable care provider.
Comparison shopping for medical care can be time-consuming. But for patients facing elective procedures, the effort can pay off — sometimes saving thousands of dollars.
“This was a learning experience for me,” Rangel said, “and I hope it will be for other people, too.”



Bill of the Month is a crowdsourced investigation by KFF Health News and The Washington Post’s Well+Being that dissects and explains medical bills. Since 2018, this series has helped many patients and readers get their medical bills reduced, and it has been cited in statehouses, at the U.S. Capitol, and at the White House. name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio cities brace for possible uptick of ICE activity after protected status ends for Haitians
description: Ohio cities with big Haitian populations are preparing for a possible uptick of United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement after temporary protected status for Haitians ended this week.  Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church, said he recently heard of a new tactic ICE is using in Springfield.  “I received a call from a […]
text:
Signs of support for Haitians in Springfield after temporary protected status for Haitians ended on July 27. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).  Ohio cities with big Haitian populations are preparing for a possible uptick of United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement after temporary protected status for Haitians ended this week. 
Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church, said he recently heard of a new tactic ICE is using in Springfield. 
“I received a call from a leader in our community who said that what’s happening is Haitians in Springfield are getting letters asking them to report to Homeland Security and ICE down in Cincinnati,” he said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“They’re asked to report in, and what I was told is that once they get there, they are asked to wear an ankle bracelet and report back in a month.”
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last month that President Donald Trump can end legal status for Haitians who’ve fled the violence in their home country.
About 330,000 Haitians are living in the United States with Temporary Protected Status (TPS), a program that allows people from specific countries in conflict or facing natural disasters the chance to live and work in the United States for a set period of time.
About 30,000 Haitians with temporary status live in central Ohio and 15,000 Haitians live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship, and other legal status.
“The federal officials are now telling us that they do not have any plans,” Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who was born in Springfield, told reporters on Wednesday. 
“They’ve received no instructions to have any kind of raids in Springfield. Now that can change, but they did tell us they’ve heard nothing.” 
Mike and his wife Fran DeWine help support the Becky DeWine School in Haiti, named after their late daughter, but the school had to close due to gang activity in 2024. 
“It’s a mistake to say that (Haitians) can no longer stay in this country,” DeWine said.
Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church, speaks in support of Haitians living in Springfield during a press conference. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
“I think that the people who have come here to work, the Haitians who came to Springfield, were filling jobs that had not been filled before. They are part of the resurgence of Springfield.”
Springfield Mayor Rob Rue said he has not received information from ICE about enforcement operations. 
“I hope Congress will seize this opportunity to modernize our immigration system in a way that upholds the rule of law, strengthens our economy and reflects the values that have long made the United States strong,” he said in a statement. 
Maqueli Eldredge, a paralegal at Legal Immigration Services in Dublin, anticipates an uptick of ICE activity as a result of TPS ending. 
ICE detained more than 280 people in Columbus in December during Operation Buckeye. 
“I’m afraid it might turn into that, but I hope not,” Eldredge said.
“We might see some large numbers, but it wouldn’t be as public as it was in December.”
She said ICE has changed their tactics from detaining people in public spaces like courthouses and in the streets to instead knocking on people’s doors and detaining people where they live. 
Columbus Mayor Andrew Ginther called forcing Haitians back to Haiti “irresponsible and inhumane.”
“Our immigrant and refugee neighbors make positive contributions to our community through their unique perspectives, workplace contributions and participation in our economy,” he said in a statement. 
“We cannot prevent federal operations from happening in our city, and federal officers do not communicate their plans with us.”
Ruby is asking ICE not to come to Springfield.
“We will encourage people to protest peacefully,” he said. “There are many who are willing to place themselves between ICE and people who are targets for detainment and deportation.” 
Haitians were initially granted temporary protected status after Haiti’s earthquake in 2010 killed 222,570 people. The Biden administration extended Temporary Protected Status to Haitians in 2021 after the assassination of Haiti President Jovenel Moïse. 
The U.S. Department of State currently has a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited health care,” according to the state department. A top security official and chief of staff to the nation’s defense minister was kidnapped last month. 
“I’ve talked to families who are so afraid of going back to Haiti,” Ruby said. 
“Rape is endemic in Haiti right now, and if all of the Haitians who are in Springfield who have been on TPS were sent back to Haiti, some of the teenage girls who have sat in our city schools next to our own children are probably going to be subject to that.” 
Signs of support for Haitians in Springfield after temporary protected status ended on July 27. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
Springfield experienced a shrinking population for decades as manufacturing jobs disappeared, but Haitian immigrants have grown Clark County’s workforce by more than 10,000 workers. 
The Clark County city became a flashpoint in the 2024 Election when Trump and JD Vance spread racist lies about Haitian immigrants there.
Rev. Michelle Boomgaard of Christ Episcopal Church talked about the growth Springfield had because of the Haitians. 
“We are seeing buildings long shuttered now open,” she said. “We are seeing new vibrancy in our communities.”
Deporting Haitians in Springfield would eliminate roughly $300 million in annual spending from Clark County, with an estimated economic loss projected to exceed $400 million.
Haitians also contribute millions of dollars in Columbus, said Yola Lamarre, an advocate with the Haitian Community Network.
“We’re going to see that impact because of this job loss,” she said. “We’re going to see the shortages in the healthcare industry and other industries that Haitians mostly populate.” 
Haitians in Ohio lost their work permits when TPS expired on Monday.
More than 1,000 children born in Springfield with American citizenship have Haitian parents. 
“I think that many of them are planning on taking their children with them, even if (the children) are U.S. citizens and have the protection,” Ruby said. 
Haitian parents are now faced with the choice of leaving their children or taking them back to Haiti “where they could be kidnapped, raped, or murdered,” Ruby said. 
“Imagine the dilemma that that is for mom and dad who love their kids, and that’s the situation that we have created for Haitian families right now, and it’s completely unnecessary.”
The Ohio Department of Children and Youth gave a grant to the Nehemiah Foundation and the Department of Jobs and Family Services to create a respite care network, said Tim Voltz of Champion City Church in Springfield. 
“There would be temporary places for those children to go, so they wouldn’t end up in a facility or detained somewhere,” he said. 
At least 18 families are part of the network, which can host children for up to 14 days at a time, Voltz said. 
“It is not a permanent solution,” he said. 
“It is only meant to provide a place for them while the state and the parents themselves and everyone tries to figure out how to reunite the parents of their children, or place them with kin. … The goal was to keep children from being shipped all over the state to foster care placements.” 
The emotional burden is overwhelming for Haitian families, said Jimmy Pierre of Gospel Grace Baptist Church in Springfield.
“Parents worry about what the future holds,” he said. 
“Some are having difficulty sleeping because they fear separation from their spouses or children. Many are dealing with anxiety, depression, and emotional exhaustion as they try to care for their families while living with uncertainty.”
Haitians can apply for asylum, but the Trump administration put an indefinite freeze on processing all asylum applications at the end of 2025.
About 4% of asylum cases are being approved, Ruby said. 
“Applying for asylum isn’t really a realistic option,” he said. 
At the federal level, the U.S. House voted in April to extend TPS for Haitians through 2029. The bill is now in the U.S. Senate, but the White House said President Donald Trump would veto the bill. 
U.S. Senators introduced an identical bill last month. 
“It’s time to put our ideology aside and focus on saving the lives of families,” Ruby said.
